co2-drying-purification.description: Carbon dioxide generated from calcium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid is contaminated with hydrogen chloride gas and water vapour; the gas stream is first passed through saturated sodium bicarbonate solution to remove hydrogen chloride, then through concentrated sulfuric acid for drying.
objectives: Understand the sources of impurities in the product gas of a preparation reaction
Master the techniques of scrubbing impurities in a gas washing bottle and drying with concentrated sulfuric acid
Recognise the correct connection orientation of a gas washing bottle: gas enters through the long tube and exits through the short tube

hcl-preparation.title: Laboratory Preparation of Hydrogen Chloride
hcl-preparation.description: Hydrogen chloride gas is prepared by gently heating sodium chloride solid with concentrated sulfuric acid. The gas forms a white mist in moist air and dissolves in water to yield hydrochloric acid.
objectives: Understand the principle of using a non-volatile acid to produce a volatile acid
Recognize the high solubility and acidic character of hydrogen chloride
Learn the upward displacement of air method for gas collection

nh3-from-ammonium-sulfate.title: Preparation of Ammonia Gas from Ammonium Sulfate and Slaked Lime
nh3-from-ammonium-sulfate.description: Ammonia gas is prepared by heating a mixture of ammonium sulfate and calcium hydroxide. The gas is identified using moistened red litmus paper, illustrating the general reaction between ammonium salts and bases upon heating.
objectives: Master the preparation of ammonia gas by reacting an ammonium salt with a base
Use moistened litmus paper to identify ammonia gas
Understand why the test tube is positioned mouth-downward to prevent condensed water from flowing back

nh3-tail-gas-absorption.title: Identification of Ammonia Gas and Tail-Gas Absorption
nh3-tail-gas-absorption.description: Ammonia gas is generated by heating ammonium chloride with calcium hydroxide. It is identified with moistened litmus paper. At the outlet end, the delivery tube is held close to the surface of distilled water to absorb excess gas while preventing suck-back.
objectives: Master the method for identifying ammonia gas
Learn tail-gas absorption techniques for highly soluble gases
Understand the function of anti-suck-back apparatus

chlorine-oxidize-ki.title: Displacement Reaction Between Chlorine and Potassium Iodide
chlorine-oxidize-ki.description: When chlorine is bubbled into a solution of potassium iodide containing starch, the solution turns blue, demonstrating that chlorine displaces iodine and confirming that chlorine has a stronger oxidizing power than iodine.
objectives: Verify the strong oxidizing power of chlorine
Understand displacement reactions among halogens and the order of their oxidizing abilities
Master the use of starch to detect iodine

chlorine-bleaching-mechanism.title: Investigation of the Bleaching Action of Chlorine
chlorine-bleaching-mechanism.description: Dry chlorine and moist chlorine are each directed onto red litmus paper: the dry gas causes no colour change, while the moist gas causes decolouration. This demonstrates that the bleaching agent is hypochlorous acid, formed when chlorine reacts with water.
objectives: Recognize that chlorine itself has no bleaching action
Understand that hypochlorous acid is the active bleaching component
Appreciate the design principles of controlled comparative experiments

chlorine-tail-gas-naoh.title: Tail-Gas Treatment for Chlorine
chlorine-tail-gas-naoh.description: After chlorine has been generated or used, excess gas is absorbed by passing it through sodium hydroxide solution, preventing air pollution. This illustrates the general principle of treating toxic tail gases before release.
objectives: Master the absorption of chlorine tail gas using alkaline solution
Understand the environmental requirement that toxic gases must not be vented directly into the atmosphere
Identify the products formed when chlorine reacts with a base

so2-reduce-kmno4.title: Verification of the Reducing Property of Sulfur Dioxide
so2-reduce-kmno4.description: Sulfur dioxide is prepared from sodium sulfite and dilute sulfuric acid, then bubbled into purple potassium permanganate solution. Decolouration of the solution confirms the reducing property of sulfur dioxide.
objectives: Master the preparation of sulfur dioxide
Verify its reducing property by decolourising potassium permanganate solution
Distinguish between decolouration caused by reducing action and that caused by bleaching

so2-from-bisulfite.title: Preparation of Sulfur Dioxide from Sodium Bisulfite
so2-from-bisulfite.description: Sulfur dioxide is prepared by reacting sodium bisulfite with dilute sulfuric acid. Moistened litmus paper is used to confirm the acidic character of the gas, introducing an alternative route for its preparation.
objectives: Master the preparation of sulfur dioxide from a bisulfite salt and an acid
Verify the acidic nature of sulfur dioxide
Recognise that the same gas can be prepared from different starting materials

feoh2-air-oxidation.title: Preparation and Color Changes of Iron(II) Hydroxide
feoh2-air-oxidation.description: Iron(II) sulfate reacts with sodium hydroxide to form a white iron(II) hydroxide precipitate, which rapidly turns gray-green in air and ultimately becomes the red-brown iron(III) hydroxide.
objectives: Prepare iron(II) hydroxide
Observe the successive color changes
Understand why Fe²⁺ is readily oxidized by atmospheric oxygen

agcl-light-darkening.title: Photodarkening of Silver Chloride
agcl-light-darkening.description: Silver nitrate reacts with potassium chloride to produce a white silver chloride precipitate, which gradually darkens to gray-black upon exposure to light, illustrating the photosensitivity of silver halides.
objectives: Observe the formation of a white precipitate
Recognize the photosensitivity of silver halides
Connect the observation to photography and photosensitive materials

halide-fractional-precipitation.title: Fractional Precipitation of Halide Ions
halide-fractional-precipitation.description: Silver nitrate solution is added dropwise to a mixture of sodium chloride, potassium bromide, and potassium iodide; the precipitates form in order of increasing solubility product — yellow silver iodide first, then pale-yellow silver bromide, and finally white silver chloride.
objectives: Understand the principle of fractional precipitation
Compare the solubility products of silver halides
Observe the sequence of precipitate colors

common-ion-effect-agcl.title: Effect of the Common-Ion Effect on the Solubility of Silver Chloride
common-ion-effect-agcl.description: A silver chloride precipitate is first prepared from silver nitrate and sodium chloride; hydrochloric acid is then added to introduce additional chloride ions, demonstrating that the common-ion effect decreases the solubility of silver chloride.
objectives: Recognize the common-ion effect
Analyze the solubility-product equilibrium of a precipitate
Relate the observation to the direction of shift in the solubility-product expression

precipitate-washing-filtration.title: Filtration and Washing of a Precipitate
precipitate-washing-filtration.description: Using the white barium sulfate precipitate obtained from barium chloride and sodium sulfate as a model system, students practice filtration and precipitate washing, then test whether the washing is complete.
objectives: Perform filtration according to standard laboratory procedure
Master the technique for washing a precipitate
Judge whether a precipitate has been washed clean

hydroxide-color-identification.title: Identification of Ions by the Color of Their Hydroxide Precipitates
hydroxide-color-identification.description: Sodium hydroxide is added to a mixture of iron(III) chloride and copper(II) sulfate; the red-brown and blue precipitates formed are used to identify iron(III) and copper(II) ions, respectively.
objectives: Identify ions on the basis of precipitate color
Observe the red-brown and blue precipitates
Write the corresponding ionic equations

barium-salts-acid-solubility.title: Comparison of the Acid Solubility of Barium Sulfate and Barium Carbonate
barium-salts-acid-solubility.description: Barium chloride is reacted separately with sodium sulfate and sodium carbonate to obtain white precipitates of barium sulfate and barium carbonate; hydrochloric acid is then added to each to compare their solubilities in acid.
objectives: Compare the acid solubility of the two precipitates
Distinguish between sulfate and carbonate ions
Understand the difference in stability between sparingly soluble salts

cuoh2-thermal-decomposition.title: Thermal Decomposition of Copper(II) Hydroxide
cuoh2-thermal-decomposition.description: Copper(II) sulfate reacts with sodium hydroxide to yield a blue copper(II) hydroxide precipitate, which decomposes on heating to give black copper(II) oxide.
objectives: Prepare copper(II) hydroxide
Observe the phenomenon of thermal decomposition
Recognize the formation of copper(II) oxide

feoh3-ignition-oxide.title: Preparation of iron(III) oxide by ignition of iron(III) hydroxide
feoh3-ignition-oxide.description: iron(III) chloride reacts with sodium hydroxide to form a reddish-brown precipitate of iron(III) hydroxide, which is then converted to red-brown iron(III) oxide by filtration and ignition.
objectives: Prepare iron(III) hydroxide
Observe decomposition by ignition
Understand the formation of iron(III) oxide

carbonate-vs-sulfate-barium.title: Using barium salts to distinguish sulfate from carbonate
carbonate-vs-sulfate-barium.description: Adding barium chloride to both sodium sulfate and sodium carbonate solutions yields white precipitates in each case; subsequent addition of hydrochloric acid dissolves only the barium carbonate with evolution of gas, thereby distinguishing the two anions.
objectives: Distinguish sulfate from carbonate ions
Observe the different behaviour of the precipitates in acid
Understand how interfering ions are eliminated

sequential-anion-detection.title: Separation and identification of chloride and sulfate ions
sequential-anion-detection.description: In a mixture containing sodium chloride and sodium sulfate, excess barium chloride is first added to precipitate and remove the sulfate ions; after filtration, silver nitrate and dilute nitric acid are used to test for chloride ions.
objectives: Design a separation and identification procedure
Eliminate interference from sulfate ions
Master the correct sequence of analytical tests

volhard-chloride-titration.title: Determination of chloride by the Volhard back-titration method
volhard-chloride-titration.description: In a nitric-acid-acidified solution of sodium chloride, excess silver nitrate is added to precipitate the chloride ions; iron(III) sulfate is used as indicator, and the excess silver ions are back-titrated with potassium thiocyanate until a red colour appears at the endpoint.
objectives: Master the Volhard precipitation titration method
Identify the titration endpoint
Calculate the chloride content of the sample

copper-hydroxide-anion-independence.title: Comparison of copper(II) hydroxide prepared from different copper salts
copper-hydroxide-anion-independence.description: Copper(II) sulfate, copper(II) chloride, and copper(II) nitrate are each reacted with sodium hydroxide, all yielding the same blue copper(II) hydroxide precipitate, demonstrating that the precipitate is determined solely by the copper(II) ion.
objectives: Compare the reactions of different copper(II) salts
Understand the nature of ionic reactions
Observe the identical blue precipitate formed in each case

seawater-magnesium-extraction.title: Simulation of magnesium extraction from seawater
seawater-magnesium-extraction.description: In a simulated seawater magnesium extraction, calcium hydroxide is added to a solution of magnesium chloride to produce a white precipitate of magnesium hydroxide.
objectives: Understand the process of extracting magnesium from seawater
Prepare magnesium hydroxide
Recognise the rationale for choosing an inexpensive base

caco3-acid-dissolution.title: Formation and acid dissolution of calcium carbonate precipitate
caco3-acid-dissolution.description: Sodium carbonate reacts with calcium chloride to form a white precipitate of calcium carbonate; subsequent addition of hydrochloric acid dissolves the precipitate with evolution of carbon dioxide.
objectives: Observe the formation and dissolution of a precipitate
Understand the properties of calcium carbonate
Connect the reaction to natural phenomena such as limestone caves and scale formation

ferrous-ferric-hydroxide-comparison.title: Comparison of iron(II) and iron(III) hydroxides
ferrous-ferric-hydroxide-comparison.description: iron(II) sulfate and iron(III) chloride are reacted separately with sodium hydroxide; the white, readily discoloured iron(II) hydroxide is compared with the reddish-brown iron(III) hydroxide.
objectives: Compare the two oxidation states of iron
Observe the difference in precipitate colour
Understand the susceptibility of iron(II) to oxidation

baso4-from-nitrate.title: Preparation of Barium Sulfate Precipitate from Barium Nitrate
baso4-from-nitrate.description: Barium nitrate reacts with potassium sulfate to produce a white barium sulfate precipitate that is insoluble in dilute nitric acid.
objectives: Prepare barium sulfate by precipitation
Recognize barium salts as a reagent for testing sulfate ions
Observe a white precipitate that is insoluble in acid

baso4-from-copper-sulfate.title: Selective Precipitation of Sulfate from Copper(II) Sulfate Solution
baso4-from-copper-sulfate.description: When barium chloride is added to a blue copper(II) sulfate solution, a white barium sulfate precipitate forms while the solution remains blue, demonstrating that only the sulfate ions have been selectively removed.
objectives: Understand the concept of selective precipitation
Observe the contrast between precipitate formation and solution color
Recognize that ions can react independently of one another

kmno4-fecl2.title: Oxidation of Iron(II) Chloride by Potassium Permanganate
kmno4-fecl2.description: When potassium permanganate is added dropwise to an acidic iron(II) chloride solution, the purple-red color fades and the pale green solution turns yellow-brown, illustrating the strong oxidizing power of potassium permanganate in converting iron(II) to iron(III).
objectives: Observe the decolorization of the purple-red permanganate color
Recognize the oxidation of iron(II) ions
Write the corresponding ionic equation

kmno4-h2o2.title: Reaction of Potassium Permanganate with Hydrogen Peroxide
kmno4-h2o2.description: When hydrogen peroxide is added dropwise to an acidic potassium permanganate solution, the purple-red color fades and gas bubbles are produced, showing that hydrogen peroxide acts as a reducing agent in this reaction and is oxidized to release oxygen.
objectives: Observe decolorization and gas evolution
Recognize the reducing character of hydrogen peroxide
Understand how potassium permanganate serves as a self-indicating reagent

k2cr2o7-fe2.title: Oxidation of Iron(II) Sulfate by Potassium Dichromate
k2cr2o7-fe2.description: When acidic potassium dichromate is added dropwise to an iron(II) sulfate solution, the orange color changes to green, demonstrating that potassium dichromate oxidizes iron(II) ions while itself being reduced to chromium(III).
objectives: Observe the color change from orange to green
Recognize the change in chromium oxidation state
Write the balanced redox equation

k2cr2o7-ethanol.title: Oxidation of Ethanol by Potassium Dichromate
k2cr2o7-ethanol.description: Acidic potassium dichromate turns from orange to green upon contact with ethanol, illustrating the oxidation of the alcohol and providing the chemical basis for breath-alcohol testing.
objectives: Observe the color change from orange to green
Recognize the oxidation of ethanol
Connect the reaction to the principle of drink-driving breath tests

thiosulfate-iodine-titration.title: Titration of Iodine with Sodium Thiosulfate (Iodometric Method)
thiosulfate-iodine-titration.description: A standard sodium thiosulfate solution is used to titrate iodine solution; starch indicator is added near the endpoint to produce a blue color, and the titration is complete when the blue color just disappears, illustrating the quantitative principles of the iodometric method.
objectives: Master the iodometric titration technique
Use starch solution as an indicator to identify the endpoint
Calculate the iodine content from titration data

h2o2-oxidize-ki.title: Oxidation of Potassium Iodide by Hydrogen Peroxide
h2o2-oxidize-ki.description: Under acidic conditions, hydrogen peroxide oxidizes potassium iodide to liberate iodine; the addition of starch solution produces a blue color, demonstrating the oxidizing character of hydrogen peroxide.
objectives: Observe the development of blue color with starch
Recognize the oxidizing character of hydrogen peroxide
Compare this behavior with the reducing character of hydrogen peroxide observed in other reactions

bromine-fe2-oxidation.title: Oxidation of Iron(II) Ions by Bromine Water
bromine-fe2-oxidation.description: Bromine water is added to an iron(II) sulfate solution; the orange color fades, and the subsequent addition of potassium thiocyanate produces a red coloration, confirming that bromine has oxidized iron(II) ions to iron(III) ions.
objectives: Observe the decolorization caused by oxidation
Confirm the presence of iron(III) ions using a color test
Compare the relative oxidizing strengths of the reagents

so2-kmno4-decolor.title: Decolorization of Potassium Permanganate by Sulfur Dioxide
so2-kmno4-decolor.description: Sulfur dioxide is bubbled into an acidified potassium permanganate solution; the purple-red color fades, demonstrating the reducing property of sulfur dioxide and distinguishing this effect from bleaching.
objectives: Recognize the reducing property of SO₂
Distinguish reduction from bleaching
Write the corresponding ionic equation

copper-concentrated-sulfuric-acid.title: Reaction of Copper with Concentrated Sulfuric Acid
copper-concentrated-sulfuric-acid.description: Copper strip is heated with concentrated sulfuric acid; a pungent gas is evolved and the solution turns blue, illustrating the strong oxidizing property of concentrated sulfuric acid (carry out in a fume hood).
objectives: Recognize the oxidizing property of concentrated sulfuric acid
Observe gas evolution and the blue coloration of the solution
Understand the difference between concentrated and dilute sulfuric acid

silver-nitric-acid.title: Reaction of Silver with Nitric Acid
silver-nitric-acid.description: Silver reacts with dilute nitric acid to give a colorless solution and evolves a gas, demonstrating that nitric acid can dissolve the relatively inactive metal silver through its strong oxidizing property (carry out in a fume hood).
objectives: Recognize the oxidizing property of nitric acid
Observe gas evolution
Understand the limitations of the metal activity series

halogen-displacement-cl-i.title: Displacement of Iodine by Chlorine Water
halogen-displacement-cl-i.description: Chlorine water is added to a potassium iodide solution, displacing iodine; the addition of starch produces a blue coloration, confirming that the oxidizing power of chlorine is greater than that of iodine.
objectives: Verify the relative reactivity of chlorine and iodine
Observe the iodine–starch color reaction
Understand the pattern of halogen displacement

halogen-oxidizing-power.title: Comparison of Oxidizing Power among the Halogens
halogen-oxidizing-power.description: Chlorine water is used to displace bromine from potassium bromide, and bromine water is used to displace iodine from potassium iodide; starch is used as an indicator, and the results are used to establish the decreasing order of oxidizing power: chlorine > bromine > iodine.
objectives: Compare the oxidizing power of the halogens
Design and conduct a controlled comparative experiment
Summarize the trend of decreasing oxidizing power down the group

fe3-iodide-oxidation.title: Oxidation of Iodide Ions by Iron(III) Ions
fe3-iodide-oxidation.description: Potassium iodide is added to an iron(III) chloride solution; the brown-yellow color deepens as iodine is produced, and the subsequent addition of starch gives a blue coloration, confirming that iron(III) ions can oxidize iodide ions.
objectives: Recognize the oxidizing property of Fe³⁺
Observe the formation of iodine
Compare the relative oxidizing strengths of the species involved

sulfite-iodine-reduction.title: Decolorization of Iodine Solution by Sodium Sulfite
sulfite-iodine-reduction.description: Sodium sulfite is added to a blue iodine–starch solution; the blue color fades, confirming that sodium sulfite, acting as a reducing agent, reduces iodine to iodide ions.
objectives: Recognize the reducing property of sulfite salts
Observe the disappearance of the blue color
Write the corresponding ionic equation

sulfite-kmno4-oxidation.title: Oxidation of Sodium Sulfite by Potassium Permanganate
sulfite-kmno4-oxidation.description: When sodium sulfite is added to acidified potassium permanganate solution, the purple-red colour fades, demonstrating the reducing character of sodium sulfite as it is oxidised to sulfate.
objectives: Observe the decolorisation of the purple-red solution
Recognise that sulfite is oxidised to sulfate
Write the balanced ionic equation

oxalic-acid-reducing-dichromate.title: Reduction of Potassium Dichromate by Oxalic Acid
oxalic-acid-reducing-dichromate.description: When oxalic acid is heated with acidified potassium dichromate solution, the orange colour changes to green and a gas is evolved, illustrating the reducing character of oxalic acid and the change in oxidation state of chromium.
objectives: Observe the colour change from orange to green
Recognise the reducing character of oxalic acid
Understand the reduction of chromium to the +3 state

iodine-thiosulfate-decolor.title: Reaction of Iodine with Sodium Thiosulfate
iodine-thiosulfate-decolor.description: When sodium thiosulfate solution is added dropwise to a blue iodine–starch solution, the blue colour disappears instantly, demonstrating the ability of sodium thiosulfate to reduce iodine and establishing the basis for the iodometric endpoint.
objectives: Observe the instantaneous disappearance of the blue colour
Recognise the reducing character of sodium thiosulfate
Connect the observation to the endpoint in iodometric titrations

zinc-sulfuric-hydrogen.title: Preparation of Hydrogen Gas from Zinc and Dilute Sulfuric Acid
zinc-sulfuric-hydrogen.description: Zinc granules react with dilute sulfuric acid, producing a continuous stream of bubbles of hydrogen gas accompanied by a noticeable release of heat, illustrating the laboratory preparation of hydrogen gas.
objectives: Observe gas evolution and heat release
Test for the presence of hydrogen gas
Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction

magnesium-hydrochloric-acid.title: Reaction of Magnesium Ribbon with Hydrochloric Acid
magnesium-hydrochloric-acid.description: When magnesium ribbon is placed in dilute hydrochloric acid, vigorous bubbling produces hydrogen gas and the test tube becomes noticeably warm, demonstrating the rapid reaction between an active metal and an acid.
objectives: Observe vigorous gas evolution
Perceive the exothermic nature of the reaction
Compare the reactivity of different metals

lead-hydrochloric-slow.title: Slow Reaction of Lead with Hydrochloric Acid
lead-hydrochloric-slow.description: When a lead strip is placed in dilute hydrochloric acid, only a slow and limited evolution of bubbles is observed; a layer of sparingly soluble lead chloride forms on the surface and impedes further reaction, indicating the relatively low reactivity of lead.
objectives: Observe the sluggish rate of reaction
Recognise the passivating effect of the surface layer
Locate lead in the activity series

potassium-water.title: Reaction of Potassium Metal with Water
potassium-water.description: When potassium (metal) is dropped into water containing a few drops of phenolphthalein, the reaction is more vigorous than that of sodium: the metal floats, melts, moves rapidly across the surface, and ignites with a lilac flame, turning the solution red.
objectives: Observe the vigorous reaction and lilac flame
Recognise the formation of a strongly alkaline solution
Compare the reactivity of potassium and sodium

calcium-water.title: Reaction of Calcium Metal with Water
calcium-water.description: When calcium metal is placed in water containing a few drops of phenolphthalein, hydrogen gas is evolved steadily and the formation of calcium hydroxide turns the solution red; the reaction is noticeably less violent than that of sodium.
objectives: Observe the sustained evolution of hydrogen gas
Recognise the formation of a sparingly soluble base
Compare the reactivity of different metals

sodium-potassium-water-compare.title: Comparing the Reactivity of Sodium and Potassium with Water
sodium-potassium-water-compare.description: Sodium metal and potassium (metal) are added separately to water containing phenolphthalein; potassium reacts more vigorously and ignites more readily, allowing the activity series to be ranked from the observed differences.
objectives: Compare the relative vigour of each reaction
Arrange the two metals in order of reactivity
Handle alkali metals safely and follow correct laboratory procedure

zinc-copper-sulfate.title: Displacement of Copper from Copper(II) Sulfate by Zinc
zinc-copper-sulfate.description: Zinc granules are immersed in blue copper(II) sulfate solution; red copper deposits on the surface and the blue colour fades, confirming that zinc is more reactive than copper.
objectives: Observe the displacement reaction and the accompanying colour change
Compare the reactivity of zinc and copper
Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction

magnesium-copper-sulfate.title: Displacement of Copper from Copper(II) Sulfate by Magnesium
magnesium-copper-sulfate.description: Magnesium ribbon placed in copper(II) sulfate solution rapidly produces a red copper deposit with a noticeable release of heat, and the blue colour fades markedly, illustrating the strong displacing power of an active metal.
objectives: Observe the rapid displacement reaction
Recognise the exothermic nature of the reaction
Understand the difference in reactivity between magnesium and copper

aluminum-copper-chloride.title: Displacement of Copper from Copper(II) Chloride by Aluminium
aluminum-copper-chloride.description: Polished aluminium strip placed in copper(II) chloride solution produces a red copper deposit as the blue colour disappears, demonstrating the strong reducing character of aluminium.
objectives: Observe the displacement reaction
Understand why the oxide layer must be removed by polishing
Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction

zinc-silver-nitrate.title: Displacement of Silver from Silver Nitrate by Zinc
zinc-silver-nitrate.description: Zinc granules placed in silver nitrate solution develop silvery-white dendritic crystals of silver on their surface, while the colourless solution acquires zinc salt, confirming that zinc is more reactive than silver.
objectives: Observe the growth of silver dendrites
Understand the displacement reaction in terms of electron transfer
Locate silver in the activity series

metal-order-by-salt.title: Determining Relative Reactivity by Displacement from Salt Solutions
metal-order-by-salt.description: An iron strip and a copper strip are placed separately in copper(II) sulfate solution; copper deposits on the iron strip while the copper strip shows no change, establishing that iron is more reactive than copper.
objectives: Design a controlled comparative experiment
Interpret observations to determine relative reactivity
Generalise the rule for displacement reactions

copper-dilute-nitric-acid.title: Reaction of Copper with Dilute Nitric Acid
copper-dilute-nitric-acid.description: A copper strip dissolves in dilute nitric acid to form a blue copper(II) nitrate solution, releasing colourless nitrogen monoxide that turns red-brown on contact with air, illustrating the strong oxidising character of nitric acid.
objectives: Observe the formation of the blue solution
Recognise the colour change of the evolved gas
Understand the oxidising properties of nitric acid

iron-ferric-chloride.title: Comproportionation Reaction between Iron and Iron(III) Chloride
iron-ferric-chloride.description: An iron strip placed in yellow-brown iron(III) chloride solution gradually dissolves as the solution turns pale green, because iron reduces iron(III) to iron(II).
objectives: Observe the gradual colour change of the solution
Understand the concept of a comproportionation reaction
Recognise the variable oxidation states of iron

iron-oxide-hydrochloric.title: Iron(III) Oxide Dissolved in Hydrochloric Acid
iron-oxide-hydrochloric.description: Reddish-brown iron(III) oxide gradually dissolves in dilute hydrochloric acid to produce a yellow solution, illustrating the salt-forming reaction between a metal oxide and an acid.
objectives: Observe the dissolution and resulting yellow coloration
Understand the principle of rust removal
Write the balanced chemical equation

copper-oxide-sulfuric.title: Reaction of Copper(II) Oxide with Sulfuric Acid
copper-oxide-sulfuric.description: Black copper(II) oxide dissolves in dilute sulfuric acid upon gentle warming to yield a blue copper(II) sulfate solution, demonstrating salt formation from a metal oxide.
objectives: Observe the black solid dissolving and the solution turning blue
Understand the chemical properties of metal oxides
Recognize the wet-chemical preparation of copper salts

magnesium-oxide-hydrochloric.title: Basic Oxide Properties of Magnesium Oxide
magnesium-oxide-hydrochloric.description: White magnesium oxide dissolves in dilute hydrochloric acid to give a colorless magnesium chloride solution, illustrating the reaction of a basic oxide with an acid.
objectives: Observe the dissolution of the solid
Recognize the nature of basic oxides
Write the balanced chemical equation

iron-oxygen-burning.title: Combustion of Iron in Oxygen
iron-oxygen-burning.description: A heated iron strip inserted into a gas collection bottle filled with oxygen burns vigorously with showers of sparks, producing black iron(II,III) oxide as the solid product.
objectives: Observe the characteristic shower of sparks
Identify the combustion product
Understand the purpose of placing sand at the bottom of the bottle

copper-air-heating.title: Blackening of Copper upon Heating in Air
copper-air-heating.description: A bright copper strip heated over an alcohol lamp undergoes surface oxidation by oxygen to form black copper(II) oxide, illustrating the gradual oxidation of metals.
objectives: Observe the surface turning black
Recognize the formation of copper(II) oxide
Understand the oxidation of metals

sodium-copper-sulfate-solution.title: Sodium Metal Added to Copper(II) Sulfate Solution
sodium-copper-sulfate-solution.description: When sodium metal is added to a copper(II) sulfate solution, it first reacts vigorously with water to evolve hydrogen gas and form sodium hydroxide, which then reacts with copper(II) sulfate to produce a blue precipitate; copper is not displaced directly by sodium.
objectives: Observe gas evolution and the formation of a blue precipitate
Understand that sodium reacts with water preferentially
Distinguish the displacement rules for reactive metals

metal-flame-color.title: Flame Tests of Metal Ions
metal-flame-color.description: Samples of sodium chloride, calcium chloride, and potassium sulfate are each ignited on a wire loop; the characteristic flame colorations — yellow for sodium, brick-red for calcium, and violet for potassium — are used to identify the respective metal ions.
objectives: Observe the characteristic flame colorations
Master the correct procedure for flame tests
Identify metal elements by their flame colors

formic-acid-silver-mirror.title: Silver Mirror Reaction of Formic Acid
formic-acid-silver-mirror.description: Because formic acid contains an aldehyde group, it reacts with Tollens' reagent upon water bath heating to deposit a bright silver mirror on the inner wall of the test tube, demonstrating the reducing character of formic acid. The silver ammonia solution is freshly prepared by combining silver nitrate with aqueous ammonia.
objectives: Recognize the reducing properties of formic acid
Observe the formation of the silver mirror
Understand the characteristic reaction of the aldehyde group

formic-acid-methyl-ester.title: Preparation of Methyl Formate
formic-acid-methyl-ester.description: Formic acid and methanol undergo esterification in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid as a catalyst upon heating, yielding the fragrant ester methyl formate. This experiment introduces the esterification of carboxylic acids with alcohols.
objectives: Understand the esterification reaction
Understand the catalytic dehydration role of concentrated sulfuric acid
Recognize the reversibility of esterification

acetic-acid-methyl-ester.title: Preparation of Methyl Acetate
acetic-acid-methyl-ester.description: Acetic acid and methanol undergo esterification in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid to give methyl acetate. Comparison with ethyl acetate illustrates how different alcohols yield different ester products.
objectives: Reinforce understanding of the esterification reaction
Compare the ester products obtained from different alcohols
Understand the role of a catalyst

acetic-acid-carbonate.title: Reaction of Acetic Acid with Sodium Carbonate
acetic-acid-carbonate.description: Adding acetic acid to a sodium carbonate solution produces vigorous effervescence, demonstrating that acetic acid is a stronger acid than carbonic acid and introducing the acidic character of carboxylic acids.
objectives: Recognize the acidic properties of carboxylic acids
Compare the relative strengths of different acids
Observe the evolution of carbon dioxide

citric-acid-bicarbonate.title: Effervescent Reaction of Citric Acid with Sodium Bicarbonate
citric-acid-bicarbonate.description: Citric acid dissolved in water reacts with sodium bicarbonate to release carbon dioxide, producing vigorous effervescence. This experiment connects to the working principle of effervescent tablets.
objectives: Recognize the acidic properties of polyprotic carboxylic acids
Observe the effervescent phenomenon
Relate the reaction to everyday consumer products

phenol-weak-acidity.title: Weak Acidity of Phenol
phenol-weak-acidity.description: A turbid phenol suspension becomes clear upon addition of sodium hydroxide solution, forming sodium phenoxide. Subsequent bubbling of carbon dioxide through the solution restores the turbidity as phenol precipitates out, demonstrating that phenol is a weaker acid than carbonic acid.
objectives: Recognize the weak acidic properties of phenol
Compare the acidity of phenol with that of carbonic acid
Observe dissolution and precipitation

glucose-silver-mirror.title: Silver Mirror Reaction of Glucose
glucose-silver-mirror.description: Glucose, which contains an aldehyde group, is heated in a water bath with silver–ammonia solution to deposit a bright silver mirror on the inner wall of the test tube, confirming the reducing character of glucose. The silver–ammonia solution is prepared from silver nitrate and aqueous ammonia.
objectives: Detect the presence of glucose
Observe the formation of a silver mirror
Recognize the reducing properties of carbohydrates

acetaldehyde-copper-hydroxide.title: Reaction of Acetaldehyde with Freshly Prepared Copper(II) Hydroxide
acetaldehyde-copper-hydroxide.description: Acetaldehyde is heated with freshly prepared copper(II) hydroxide, made from copper(II) sulfate and sodium hydroxide solution, to give a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide, confirming the reducing character of the aldehyde group.
objectives: Detect the aldehyde group
Observe the formation of the brick-red precipitate
Learn the correct preparation and use of freshly prepared copper(II) hydroxide

ester-hydrolysis-acid.title: Acid-Catalyzed Hydrolysis of Ethyl Acetate
ester-hydrolysis-acid.description: Ethyl acetate is heated in a water bath in the presence of dilute sulfuric acid as a catalyst, hydrolyzing to give acetic acid and ethanol. The oily upper layer gradually diminishes as hydrolysis proceeds, illustrating the hydrolysis of esters.
objectives: Understand the hydrolysis of esters
Appreciate the role of a catalyst in hydrolysis
Compare acid-catalyzed and base-catalyzed hydrolysis

ester-hydrolysis-base.title: Base-Catalyzed Hydrolysis of Ethyl Acetate
ester-hydrolysis-base.description: Ethyl acetate is hydrolyzed by heating in a sodium hydroxide solution using a water bath; the ester layer disappears more rapidly and completely than in neutral conditions, demonstrating that alkali promotes ester hydrolysis.
objectives: Understand base-catalyzed hydrolysis
Recognize the difference in extent of hydrolysis under acidic and basic conditions
Connect the experiment to the saponification reaction

ethylene-kmno4.title: Decolorization of Acidic Potassium Permanganate by Ethylene
ethylene-kmno4.description: Ethylene is bubbled into an acidic potassium permanganate solution; the purple-red color fades, demonstrating that ethylene is oxidized by potassium permanganate and confirming the presence of the carbon–carbon double bond.
objectives: Recognize the oxidation of alkenes
Distinguish between saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons
Observe the decolorization phenomenon

starch-hydrolysis.title: Hydrolysis of Starch and Identification of the Product
starch-hydrolysis.description: Starch is hydrolyzed to glucose by heating in a water bath with dilute sulfuric acid as catalyst; after neutralization with sodium hydroxide, Tollens' reagent is added and the formation of a silver mirror confirms the presence of glucose. Tollens' reagent is prepared by mixing silver nitrate with aqueous ammonia.
objectives: Understand the hydrolysis of starch
Master the procedure of neutralization followed by product identification
Verify the hydrolysis product

starch-hydrolysis-iodine.title: Monitoring the Extent of Starch Hydrolysis with Iodine
starch-hydrolysis-iodine.description: Starch is hydrolyzed using dilute sulfuric acid as catalyst; samples withdrawn at intervals are neutralized with sodium hydroxide and then tested with iodine solution — the absence of a blue color indicates that hydrolysis of the starch is complete.
objectives: Monitor the progress of hydrolysis
Master the iodine test for starch
Understand why neutralization before testing is necessary

fat-hydrolysis-acid.title: Acid-Catalyzed Hydrolysis of Fats and Oils
fat-hydrolysis-acid.description: Fats and oils are hydrolyzed by heating in a water bath with dilute sulfuric acid as catalyst, yielding higher fatty acids and glycerol; the experiment introduces acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of fats and oils and provides a comparison with the saponification reaction.
objectives: Understand the hydrolysis of fats and oils
Compare the products of acid-catalyzed and base-catalyzed hydrolysis
Understand the formation of glycerol

acetic-acid-litmus.title: Testing the Acidity of Acetic Acid
acetic-acid-litmus.description: An acetic acid solution turns purple litmus red, confirming that acetic acid is acidic and illustrating the general properties of carboxylic acids.
objectives: Test the acidity of a carboxylic acid
Observe the color change of an indicator
Recognize the general properties of carboxylic acids

ethanol-water-distillation.title: Distillation of an Ethanol–Water Mixture
ethanol-water-distillation.description: An ethanol–water mixture is distilled; the difference in boiling points between ethanol and water is exploited to collect the ethanol fraction, providing practice in the technique of distillation for separation and purification.
objectives: Master the technique of distillation
Separate components by exploiting differences in boiling point
Recognize the correct positioning of the thermometer

iodine-extraction-ccl4.title: Extraction of Iodine from Iodine Solution Using Carbon Tetrachloride
iodine-extraction-ccl4.description: Carbon tetrachloride is added to iodine solution, the mixture is shaken and allowed to stand; iodine transfers into the lower carbon tetrachloride layer, which turns purple-red, and the two layers separate clearly, providing practice in liquid–liquid extraction and the use of a separating funnel.
objectives: Understand the principle of solvent extraction
Develop proficiency in separating-funnel technique
Understand how differences in solubility govern the distribution of a solute between two immiscible solvents

salicylic-acid-recrystallization.title: Recrystallization of Salicylic Acid
salicylic-acid-recrystallization.description: Crude salicylic acid is dissolved in hot distilled water to prepare a hot saturated solution; pure crystals precipitate upon cooling. Students learn the technique of purifying organic compounds by recrystallization.
objectives: Master the recrystallization procedure
Apply the relationship between solubility and temperature
Understand recrystallization as a purification method

salicylic-acid-fecl3.title: Colorimetric Test for Salicylic Acid
salicylic-acid-fecl3.description: Addition of iron(III) chloride solution to a salicylic acid solution produces a violet coloration, indicating the presence of a phenolic hydroxyl group. Students learn the characteristic color test for phenols.
objectives: Test for the phenolic hydroxyl group
Observe the violet color reaction
Relate the color reaction to the structure of salicylic acid

ethanol-dehydration-ethylene.title: Preparation and Identification of Ethylene by Dehydration of Ethanol
ethanol-dehydration-ethylene.description: Ethanol undergoes an elimination reaction in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid when heated to approximately 170 ℃, producing ethylene. The gas is passed into bromine water, which is decolorized, confirming the formation of ethylene.
objectives: Understand the elimination reaction
Control the reaction temperature to generate ethylene
Use bromine water to identify the product

hess-law-verification.title: Verification of Hess's Law
hess-law-verification.description: The heat effects of two reaction pathways are measured separately: dissolving solid sodium hydroxide directly in hydrochloric acid, and first dissolving it in distilled water then neutralizing with hydrochloric acid. The results confirm that the enthalpy change depends only on the initial and final states.
objectives: Understand Hess's Law
Design two distinct reaction pathways
Compare the total heat effects of both pathways

quicklime-water-heat.title: Exothermic Reaction of Calcium Oxide with Water
quicklime-water-heat.description: Distilled water is added to calcium oxide, and the large amount of heat released by the reaction is observed to bring the water to the boil. Students recognize this as a typical exothermic reaction.
objectives: Identify the characteristics of an exothermic reaction
Measure the rapid rise in temperature
Connect the observation to the heat of hydration in construction materials

metal-acid-exothermic.title: Exothermic Effect of the Reaction Between a Metal and an Acid
metal-acid-exothermic.description: Zinc granules are allowed to react with dilute sulfuric acid in an insulated cup. The simultaneous evolution of gas and rise in solution temperature are recorded, illustrating the exothermic nature of metal–acid reactions.
objectives: Measure the heat released during the reaction
Correlate gas evolution with the rise in temperature
Understand the origin of the exothermic effect

ethanol-combustion-heat.title: Determination of the Combustion Heat of Ethanol
ethanol-combustion-heat.description: Ethanol is ignited and burned completely in oxygen; a calorimeter is used to measure the heat released, from which the combustion heat is calculated.
objectives: Determine the combustion heat experimentally
Analyze the heat calculation procedure
Evaluate sources of heat loss

sulfuric-dilution-heat.title: Heat Released upon Dilution of Concentrated Sulfuric Acid
sulfuric-dilution-heat.description: Sulfuric acid is added slowly to distilled water with stirring, and a thermometer is used to record the substantial heat released during dilution. Students understand why the correct order of mixing must be followed.
objectives: Recognize the heat released during dilution
Learn the correct and safe order of mixing
Measure the magnitude of the temperature rise

sodium-hydroxide-dissolution-heat.title: Heat Released by Dissolving Sodium Hydroxide
sodium-hydroxide-dissolution-heat.description: Sodium hydroxide pellets are dissolved in distilled water, and a thermometer is used to record the continuous rise in solution temperature, providing a quantitative understanding of the exothermic dissolution process.
objectives: Recognise that dissolution can be exothermic
Measure the change in temperature
Understand the concept of enthalpy of dissolution

ammonium-nitrate-dissolution-endotherm.title: Heat Absorbed by Dissolving Ammonium Nitrate
ammonium-nitrate-dissolution-endotherm.description: Ammonium nitrate solid is dissolved in distilled water, and the marked drop in solution temperature is observed, illustrating the energy change associated with endothermic dissolution.
objectives: Recognise that dissolution can be endothermic
Measure the extent of temperature decrease
Compare endothermic and exothermic dissolution processes

citric-bicarbonate-endotherm.title: Endothermic Reaction between Citric Acid and Sodium Bicarbonate
citric-bicarbonate-endotherm.description: Mixing a citric acid solution with sodium bicarbonate solid produces vigorous effervescence and a measurable drop in temperature, demonstrating a typical endothermic effervescent reaction.
objectives: Recognise the characteristics of an endothermic reaction
Observe the simultaneous evolution of gas and fall in temperature
Relate the observations to the working principle of effervescent tablets

neutralization-heat-comparison.title: Comparison of Neutralisation Enthalpy for Different Strong Acids and Bases
neutralization-heat-comparison.description: The temperature changes produced when hydrochloric acid and sulfuric acid are each neutralised by sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are measured separately, verifying that the enthalpy of neutralisation is essentially the same for all strong-acid–strong-base pairs.
objectives: Compare the enthalpies of neutralisation for different acid–base combinations
Understand the fundamental nature of the neutralisation enthalpy
Analyse sources of experimental error

iron-oxidation-handwarmer.title: Exothermic Oxidation of Iron in a Hand Warmer
iron-oxidation-handwarmer.description: The accelerated oxidation of an iron strip in the presence of sodium chloride solution and oxygen is exploited to construct a simple hand warmer, and the resulting temperature rise is measured.
objectives: Recognise that slow oxidation releases heat
Understand the role of the electrolyte in promoting the oxidation reaction
Relate the experiment to the design of commercial heat packs

thiosulfate-concentration-rate.title: Effect of Concentration on the Rate of the Sodium Thiosulfate Reaction
thiosulfate-concentration-rate.description: Sodium thiosulfate solutions of varying concentrations are each reacted with dilute sulfuric acid, and the time required for the precipitated sulfur to obscure a reference mark beneath the vessel is used to compare reaction rates.
objectives: Investigate the effect of concentration on reaction rate
Apply the turbidity-timing method to rate measurement
Plot and interpret the relationship between concentration and rate

h2o2-catalyst-comparison.title: Comparison of Different Catalysts for the Decomposition of Hydrogen Peroxide
h2o2-catalyst-comparison.description: Manganese(IV) oxide and iron(III) chloride are added separately to hydrogen peroxide solution, and the effectiveness of each catalyst in accelerating oxygen evolution is compared.
objectives: Compare the catalytic effectiveness of different substances
Recognise that catalytic activity is selective
Record and compare the rate of oxygen production quantitatively

permanganate-oxalate-temperature.title: Effect of Temperature on the Rate of the Potassium Permanganate–Oxalic Acid Reaction
permanganate-oxalate-temperature.description: Acidified potassium permanganate solution is reacted with oxalic acid at different water bath temperatures, and the time required for the purple colour to discharge is used to compare reaction rates.
objectives: Investigate the effect of temperature on reaction rate
Use decolourisation time as a measure of reaction rate
Apply the method of controlled variables

permanganate-oxalate-autocatalysis.title: Autocatalysis and Activation Energy in the Potassium Permanganate–Oxalic Acid Reaction
permanganate-oxalate-autocatalysis.description: Observe how the reaction between acidic potassium permanganate and oxalic acid proceeds slowly at first, then accelerates sharply as products accumulate, illustrating autocatalysis; use this behaviour to discuss activation energy.
objectives: Recognise the phenomenon of autocatalysis
Understand the concept of activation energy
Analyse how reaction rate changes over time

iodine-clock-reaction.title: Measuring Reaction Rate Using the Iodine Clock Reaction
iodine-clock-reaction.description: Under acidic conditions, hydrogen peroxide oxidises potassium iodide to produce iodine; once the sodium thiosulfate present is consumed, the solution turns blue suddenly in the presence of starch, allowing the reaction rate to be determined.
objectives: Observe the iodine clock reaction
Determine the reaction rate quantitatively
Understand the concept of the rate-determining step

surface-area-zinc-rate.title: Effect of Particle Size on the Rate of Reaction Between Zinc and Acid
surface-area-zinc-rate.description: React intact zinc granules and finely crushed zinc with dilute sulfuric acid of equal concentration, and compare how the contact surface area affects the rate of gas evolution.
objectives: Investigate the effect of contact surface area on reaction rate
Apply controlled-variable experimental design
Record and compare rates of gas evolution

pressure-equilibrium-no2.title: Effect of Pressure on the Nitrogen Dioxide Equilibrium
pressure-equilibrium-no2.description: Seal a mixture of nitrogen dioxide and dinitrogen tetroxide at equilibrium in a syringe, then compress or extend the plunger to change the pressure, and observe the resulting changes in colour intensity.
objectives: Recognise the effect of pressure on chemical equilibrium
Observe colour changes as evidence of equilibrium shift
Apply Le Chatelier's principle to interpret the observations

esterification-equilibrium.title: Reversible Equilibrium in Esterification
esterification-equilibrium.description: React acetic acid with ethanol under sulfuric acid catalysis to produce a fruity-smelling ester; recognise that esterification is a reversible reaction and investigate methods of improving yield.
objectives: Recognise the reversible nature of esterification
Understand the concept of esterification equilibrium
Discuss practical measures to increase product yield

dichromate-chromate-equilibrium.title: Equilibrium Shift Between Dichromate and Chromate Ions
dichromate-chromate-equilibrium.description: Add sodium hydroxide and sulfuric acid separately to a potassium dichromate solution, and observe the interconversion between the orange colour of dichromate and the yellow colour of chromate, illustrating the effect of concentration on equilibrium.
objectives: Observe the shift of chemical equilibrium
Recognise the effect of concentration on equilibrium position
Apply Le Chatelier's principle to explain the colour changes

carbonic-acid-reversible.title: Reversible Reaction of Carbon Dioxide Dissolving in Water
carbonic-acid-reversible.description: Bubble carbon dioxide through distilled water containing litmus until the indicator turns red, confirming the formation of carbonic acid; then heat the solution to restore the original colour, demonstrating reversibility.
objectives: Recognise the reversible nature of the reaction
Observe the colour change and its reversal
Understand how heating shifts the equilibrium in the reverse direction

fe2-identification.title: Identification of Iron(II) Ions
fe2-identification.description: Add sodium hydroxide dropwise to an iron(II) sulfate solution containing Fe²⁺ ions; a white precipitate forms initially, turns grey-green rapidly, and finally becomes reddish-brown, providing confirmatory evidence for the presence of iron(II) ions.
objectives: Master the procedure for testing for Fe²⁺
Observe the sequence of colour changes in the precipitate
Distinguish between the two common oxidation states of iron

calcium-ion-identification.title: Identification of Calcium Ions
calcium-ion-identification.description: Adding sodium carbonate to a calcium chloride solution produces a white precipitate of calcium carbonate that is insoluble in water, thereby confirming the presence of calcium ions.
objectives: Master the procedure for detecting Ca²⁺
Observe the formation of a white precipitate
Understand the solubility of precipitates

magnesium-ion-identification.title: Identification of Magnesium Ions
magnesium-ion-identification.description: Adding sodium hydroxide dropwise to a magnesium chloride solution produces a white precipitate of magnesium hydroxide, thereby confirming the presence of magnesium ions.
objectives: Master the procedure for detecting Mg²⁺
Observe the formation of a white precipitate
Compare the chemical properties of calcium and magnesium

silver-ion-identification.title: Identification of Silver Ions
silver-ion-identification.description: Adding sodium chloride to a silver nitrate solution produces a white precipitate of silver chloride that is insoluble in dilute nitric acid, thereby confirming the presence of silver ions.
objectives: Master the procedure for detecting Ag⁺
Observe the formation of a white precipitate
Understand that the precipitate is insoluble in acid

bromide-identification.title: Identification of Bromide Ions
bromide-identification.description: Silver nitrate and dilute nitric acid are used to test for bromide ions; formation of a pale-yellow precipitate of silver bromide that is insoluble in acid confirms their presence.
objectives: Master the procedure for detecting Br⁻
Observe the formation of a pale-yellow precipitate
Compare the colours of silver halide precipitates

iodide-identification.title: Identification of Iodide Ions
iodide-identification.description: Silver nitrate and dilute nitric acid are used to test for iodide ions; formation of a yellow precipitate of silver iodide that is insoluble in acid confirms their presence.
objectives: Master the procedure for detecting I⁻
Observe the formation of a yellow precipitate
Understand the periodic trend across the halide series

halide-differentiation.title: Differentiation of Chloride, Bromide, and Iodide Ions
halide-differentiation.description: Silver nitrate is applied separately to solutions of sodium chloride, sodium bromide, and potassium iodide; the three halide ions are distinguished by the white, pale-yellow, and yellow colours of the respective silver halide precipitates.
objectives: Distinguish among the three halide ions
Compare the colours of the precipitates formed
Master the technique of controlled comparative experiments

sulfite-identification.title: Identification of Sulfite Ions
sulfite-identification.description: Adding barium chloride to a sodium sulfite solution produces a white precipitate; subsequent addition of dilute hydrochloric acid dissolves the precipitate with evolution of a pungent gas, thereby confirming the presence of sulfite ions.
objectives: Master the procedure for detecting sulfite ions
Distinguish between sulfate and sulfite ions
Observe precipitate dissolution accompanied by gas evolution

iodine-starch-test.title: Detection of Iodine by the Starch Colour Reaction
iodine-starch-test.description: Adding starch solution to iodine solution causes an immediate blue coloration; this colour reaction between iodine and starch provides a sensitive test for the presence of iodine.
objectives: Master the procedure for detecting iodine
Observe the blue coloration produced
Understand the sensitivity of the colour reaction

gas-co2-identification.title: Identification of Carbon Dioxide Gas
gas-co2-identification.description: Dilute hydrochloric acid is reacted with sodium carbonate to generate carbon dioxide, which is then passed into a clear limewater solution; the resulting turbidity confirms the presence of carbon dioxide.
objectives: Master the procedure for identifying CO₂
Observe the turbidity that develops in limewater
Understand the principle underlying gas generation

gas-ammonia-identification.title: Identification of Ammonia Gas
gas-ammonia-identification.description: Sodium hydroxide is added to ammonium chloride and the mixture is gently heated to release ammonia gas; the gas turns moist red litmus paper blue, thereby confirming its presence.
objectives: Master the procedure for identifying ammonia gas
Observe the colour change of the litmus paper to blue
Understand the reaction between ammonium salts and bases

gas-hydrogen-identification.title: Identification of Hydrogen Gas
gas-hydrogen-identification.description: Zinc granules are reacted with dilute sulfuric acid to produce hydrogen gas; the collected gas is ignited and emits a faint popping sound, confirming both the identity and purity of the hydrogen gas.
objectives: Master the procedure for identifying hydrogen gas
Recognise the characteristic popping sound upon ignition
Understand the purity-testing operation

gas-chlorine-identification.title: Identification of Chlorine Gas
gas-chlorine-identification.description: Chlorine in chlorine water oxidises potassium iodide to liberate iodine, which then produces a blue colour with starch, thereby confirming the strong oxidising character and presence of chlorine.
objectives: Master the procedure for identifying chlorine
Understand the oxidative displacement of iodine
Observe the blue colour that develops with starch

flame-test-sodium-potassium.title: Flame-Test Identification of Sodium and Potassium Salts
flame-test-sodium-potassium.description: A platinum wire is used to introduce sodium chloride and potassium chloride separately into a flame; sodium imparts a yellow colour and potassium a violet colour. The platinum wire is cleaned with hydrochloric acid between tests.
objectives: Distinguish the flame colours of sodium and potassium
Master the procedure for cleaning the platinum wire
Understand the principle of the flame test

titration-acid-base.title: Determination of Concentration by Acid–Base Neutralisation Titration
titration-acid-base.description: Using phenolphthalein as the indicator, a sodium hydroxide standard solution of known concentration is used to titrate hydrochloric acid of unknown concentration; the sharp colour change marks the endpoint, from which the concentration is calculated.
objectives: Master the operational technique of neutralisation titration
Determine the titration endpoint from the colour change
Calculate the concentration of the analyte solution

titration-redox-kmno4.title: Oxidation–Reduction Titration with Potassium Permanganate
titration-redox-kmno4.description: Under acidic conditions provided by sulfuric acid, a potassium permanganate standard solution is used to titrate an oxalic acid solution; the endpoint is reached when the purple-red colour just fades and does not return, allowing the oxalic acid content to be calculated.
objectives: Master the technique of oxidation–reduction titration
Use the self-indicating property of potassium permanganate to determine the endpoint
Calculate the content of the reducing agent

edta-hardness-titration.title: Determination of Water Hardness by EDTA Complexometric Titration
edta-hardness-titration.description: Using Eriochrome Black T as the indicator, an EDTA standard solution is used to titrate a water sample containing calcium chloride and magnesium chloride; the endpoint is marked by the colour change from wine-red to pure blue, from which the total hardness is determined.
objectives: Master the technique of complexometric titration
Identify the colour change of the indicator at the endpoint
Calculate the total hardness due to calcium and magnesium

colorimetric-iron.title: Colorimetric Determination of Iron Content
colorimetric-iron.description: Iron(III) chloride reacts with potassium thiocyanate to form a blood-red complex. A series of standard solutions is prepared and measured with a spectrophotometer to determine the iron content of the test solution.
objectives: Master the principles of colorimetric analysis
Construct a standard calibration curve
Quantitatively determine iron content

filtration-separation.title: Separation of an Insoluble Solid by Filtration
filtration-separation.description: A mixture of calcium carbonate and sodium chloride is dissolved in distilled water and filtered; the insoluble calcium carbonate is retained on the filter paper while sodium chloride passes into the filtrate, achieving separation.
objectives: Master the technique of filtration
Apply differences in solubility to achieve separation
Follow the standard filtration procedure: one layer of filter paper flush with the funnel, liquid levels below the paper edge, and the glass rod, funnel stem, and beaker wall in proper contact

mixture-anion-identification.title: Identification of Anions in a Mixed Solution
mixture-anion-identification.description: A solution containing sodium chloride, sodium sulfate, and sodium carbonate is tested systematically using hydrochloric acid, barium chloride, silver nitrate, and nitric acid in sequence to identify the anions present.
objectives: Design a systematic analytical scheme
Eliminate interference between anions
Draw comprehensive conclusions about the composition

ion-coexistence-test.title: Experimental Investigation of Ion Coexistence
ion-coexistence-test.description: Combinations such as copper(II) sulfate with sodium hydroxide solution, barium chloride with sodium sulfate, and sodium carbonate with hydrochloric acid are tested; the formation of precipitates or evolution of gas is observed to determine which ions cannot coexist in significant concentrations in solution.
objectives: Understand the conditions required for ion coexistence
Observe precipitate formation and gas evolution
Summarize the rules governing ion incompatibility

koh-hcl-neutralization.title: Neutralization of Potassium Hydroxide with Hydrochloric Acid
koh-hcl-neutralization.description: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added dropwise to a potassium hydroxide solution containing phenolphthalein; the moment the red color disappears is noted and the rise in temperature is recorded, illustrating the exothermic nature of neutralization.
objectives: Observe the sharp color change of the indicator as a strong base is neutralized by a strong acid
Measure the temperature rise during the neutralization process
Understand that H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O is the essential reaction of neutralization

baoh2-sulfuric-double-product.title: Neutralization of Barium Hydroxide with Sulfuric Acid Accompanied by Precipitation
baoh2-sulfuric-double-product.description: Dilute sulfuric acid is added dropwise to a barium hydroxide solution; the white barium sulfate precipitate increases progressively while the electrical conductivity of the solution falls to a minimum, illustrating a neutralization in which both water and a precipitate are formed simultaneously.
objectives: Observe precipitate formation occurring concurrently with neutralization
Understand that electrical conductivity is at its lowest when ion concentrations reach their minimum
Write the net ionic equation for a neutralization reaction that involves a precipitate

nitric-naoh-neutralization.title: Acid–Base Titration of Nitric Acid with Sodium Hydroxide Solution
nitric-naoh-neutralization.description: A standard sodium hydroxide solution is used to titrate dilute nitric acid of unknown concentration; phenolphthalein serves as the indicator for the endpoint, and the molar concentration of the nitric acid is calculated from the volume relationship.
objectives: Master the technique and burette-reading procedure for acid–base titration
Identify the endpoint color change of phenolphthalein
Calculate the unknown acid concentration from the volume relationship

acetic-ammonia-weak-weak.title: Neutralization between a Weak Acid and a Weak Base
acetic-ammonia-weak-weak.description: Acetic acid and aqueous ammonia are mixed; the two weak electrolytes mutually promote each other's ionization and neutralize completely, yielding an ammonium acetate solution that is approximately neutral, which is verified with a pH meter.
objectives: Understand how a weak acid and a weak base mutually promote ionization
Verify that an ammonium acetate solution is approximately neutral
Compare the thermal effect of this reaction with that of a strong-acid–strong-base neutralization

potassium-carbonate-acid-gas.title: Gas Evolution from Potassium Carbonate and Hydrochloric Acid
potassium-carbonate-acid-gas.description: When dilute hydrochloric acid is added dropwise to solid potassium carbonate, colourless bubbles evolve vigorously and heat is released. The gas is led into limewater, which turns milky, confirming the product is carbon dioxide.
objectives: Observe the vigorous gas evolution that occurs when a carbonate reacts with an acid
Master the standard test for carbon dioxide
Write the ionic equation for the reaction of a carbonate with a strong acid

ammonium-bicarbonate-acid.title: Dual Instability of Ammonium Bicarbonate with Acid
ammonium-bicarbonate-acid.description: Ammonium bicarbonate reacts immediately with hydrochloric acid to produce carbon dioxide; the same solid, when heated separately, decomposes to release ammonia gas. This experiment provides a direct demonstration of the combined instability of both the ammonium ion and the bicarbonate ion.
objectives: Observe the gas evolution when ammonium bicarbonate reacts with an acid
Understand that both ammonium salts and bicarbonates are thermally and chemically unstable
Explain why ammonium bicarbonate fertiliser must not be mixed with alkaline materials

aluminum-hydroxide-acid-dissolve.title: Dissolution of Aluminium Hydroxide in Acid
aluminum-hydroxide-acid-dissolve.description: White solid aluminium hydroxide dissolves gradually in dilute hydrochloric acid, giving a clear solution with a noticeable release of heat. This behaviour is contrasted with its dissolution in a strong base to illustrate amphoteric character.
objectives: Observe the dissolution of a sparingly soluble base in a strong acid
Understand the basic aspect of aluminium hydroxide
Prepare for a complete understanding of amphoteric hydroxides

calcium-oxide-acid-heat.title: Vigorous Exothermic Reaction of Calcium Oxide with Hydrochloric Acid
calcium-oxide-acid-heat.description: When calcium oxide is added to dilute hydrochloric acid it dissolves rapidly and the temperature rises sharply, demonstrating that the reaction of a basic oxide with an acid releases considerably more heat than a simple neutralisation.
objectives: Observe the exothermic reaction between a basic oxide and an acid
Compare the heat effects of dissolving calcium oxide in water and in acid
Understand the classification of calcium oxide as a basic oxide

alumina-acid-slow-dissolve.title: Slow Dissolution of Aluminium Oxide in Acid
alumina-acid-slow-dissolve.description: Aluminium oxide powder dissolves only slowly in dilute hydrochloric acid; heating and stirring are required before the mixture becomes clear. This behaviour reflects the dense crystal structure and relatively high chemical inertness of aluminium oxide.
objectives: Observe the sluggish dissolution of aluminium oxide
Understand how crystal structure influences reaction rate
Recognise the status of aluminium oxide as an amphoteric oxide

sulfuric-limestone-gas.title: Self-inhibition in the Reaction of Dilute Sulfuric Acid with Limestone
sulfuric-limestone-gas.description: When dilute sulfuric acid is added to limestone, vigorous bubbling occurs initially, but gradually ceases as a layer of sparingly soluble calcium sulfate forms on the surface of the solid. This is the classical reason why sulfuric acid is not used for laboratory preparation of carbon dioxide.
objectives: Observe how gas evolution slows and eventually stops
Understand how a sparingly soluble product layer impedes the reaction
Explain why dilute hydrochloric acid rather than sulfuric acid is used in the laboratory preparation of carbon dioxide

citric-carbonate-fizz.title: Effervescent Reaction of Citric Acid with Sodium Carbonate
citric-carbonate-fizz.description: When citric acid and sodium carbonate are mixed in the presence of water, copious bubbles form immediately. This is the core formulation of effervescent tablets and demonstrates that a food-grade weak acid is capable of displacing carbonate from its salt.
objectives: Observe gas evolution when an organic weak acid reacts with a carbonate
Understand the scope of the principle that a stronger acid displaces a weaker one
Connect the reaction to the everyday application of effervescent tablets

phosphoric-limewater-turbid.title: Formation of Sparingly Soluble Calcium Phosphate from Phosphoric Acid and Limewater
phosphoric-limewater-turbid.description: When phosphoric acid is added dropwise to clear limewater, the solution turns milky white. The precipitate formed is sparingly soluble calcium phosphate, and the reaction underlies the chemistry of phosphate fertiliser production.
objectives: Observe the formation of a precipitate during a neutralisation reaction
Recognise the sparingly soluble nature of calcium phosphate
Connect the reaction to the industrial production of superphosphate fertiliser

sulfuric-ammonia-fertilizer.title: Preparation of Ammonium Sulfate by Absorption of Ammonia Gas with Sulfuric Acid
sulfuric-ammonia-fertilizer.description: Aqueous ammonia is added slowly to dilute sulfuric acid; the reaction releases heat and produces ammonium sulfate, which upon evaporation yields white crystals. This neutralisation route is the most common method of fixing nitrogen in the fertiliser industry.
objectives: Understand the industrial significance of absorbing ammonia gas with acid
Observe the heat of neutralisation and the evaporative crystallisation of the product
Calculate the theoretical yield of ammonium sulfate

litmus-ammonia-blue.title: Colour Change of Purple Litmus in Aqueous Ammonia
litmus-ammonia-blue.description: Purple litmus turns blue immediately upon addition to dilute aqueous ammonia, and the blue colour fades as the solution is diluted, demonstrating that the depth of an indicator's colour gives a rough measure of a weak base's alkalinity.
objectives: Learn the colour of litmus under alkaline conditions
Observe the effect of dilution on colour intensity
Understand that indicators can only provide a qualitative assessment of acidity or alkalinity

phenolphthalein-koh-red.title: Colour Development of Phenolphthalein in Potassium Hydroxide
phenolphthalein-koh-red.description: Phenolphthalein turns red in potassium hydroxide solution and decolourises again upon addition of excess hydrochloric acid; the transition can be repeated reversibly, illustrating the reversible colour change of indicators.
objectives: Observe the colour developed by phenolphthalein under alkaline conditions
Verify the reversibility of the indicator colour change
Understand that the colour-change range of phenolphthalein lies in the alkaline region

methyl-orange-sulfuric-red.title: Colour Change of Methyl Orange to Red in Sulfuric Acid
methyl-orange-sulfuric-red.description: Methyl orange changes from orange to red when added to dilute sulfuric acid, in contrast to its yellow colour in sodium hydroxide solution, confirming that its colour-change range falls within the acidic region.
objectives: Learn the three colour stages of methyl orange
Understand the relationship between colour-change range and the choice of indicator
Select an appropriate indicator for the titration of a strong acid against a weak base

ammonium-chloride-dissolve-cooling.title: Endothermic Cooling upon Dissolution of Ammonium Chloride
ammonium-chloride-dissolve-cooling.description: When ammonium chloride crystals dissolve in water, the thermometer reading drops noticeably and condensation forms on the outer wall of the beaker, providing direct evidence that dissolution processes are accompanied by a heat effect.
objectives: Measure the temperature decrease during the dissolution process
Distinguish between the enthalpy of dissolution and the enthalpy of reaction
Explain why ammonium salt solutions are acidic

ammonium-sulfate-base-ammonia.title: Evolution of Ammonia Gas from Ammonium Sulfate Heated with a Base
ammonium-sulfate-base-ammonia.description: When ammonium sulfate is mixed with sodium hydroxide solution and gently warmed, ammonia gas with a pungent odour is released; the gas turns moist red litmus paper blue, providing a test for ammonium salts.
objectives: Learn the method for identifying ammonium salts
Observe that ammonia gas turns moist red litmus paper blue
Explain why ammonium-based nitrogen fertilisers must not be mixed with alkaline fertilisers

nitric-carbonate-strong-weak.title: Displacement of a Weak Acid by a Strong Acid: Nitric Acid and Sodium Carbonate
nitric-carbonate-strong-weak.description: Addition of nitric acid to sodium carbonate solution produces vigorous effervescence, confirming that nitric acid is stronger than carbonic acid and providing a further illustration of the principle that a stronger acid displaces a weaker one.
objectives: Verify the principle that a strong acid displaces a weak acid
Compare the acid strengths of nitric acid and carbonic acid
Write the corresponding ionic equation

sodium-sulfite-acid-so2.title: Evolution of Sulfur Dioxide from Sodium Sulfite with Acid
sodium-sulfite-acid-so2.description: Sodium sulfite reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to release sulfur dioxide, a gas with a pungent odour that decolourises fuchsin solution; this reaction offers a convenient laboratory method for generating small quantities of sulfur dioxide.
objectives: Learn the gas-evolving reaction between sulfite salts and acids
Recognise the bleaching action of sulfur dioxide
Learn to use alkaline solution to absorb sulfur dioxide in tail-gas treatment

aluminum-naoh-hydrogen.title: Amphoteric Nature of Aluminium: Reaction with Strong Base to Produce Hydrogen Gas
aluminum-naoh-hydrogen.description: When an aluminium strip is placed in sodium hydroxide solution, hydrogen gas is evolved continuously and heat is released, demonstrating that aluminium dissolves in both acids and strong bases and providing direct evidence of its amphoteric character.
objectives: Observe the evolution of hydrogen gas when aluminium reacts with a strong base
Understand the amphoteric behaviour of aluminium
Compare the reaction rates of aluminium with acids and with bases

magnesium-oxygen-white-light.title: Combustion of Magnesium Ribbon in Oxygen
magnesium-oxygen-white-light.description: When ignited magnesium ribbon is introduced into a gas collection bottle filled with oxygen, an intensely bright white light is emitted and a white powder of magnesium oxide is produced; cobalt blue glass must be used to protect the eyes during observation.
objectives: Observe the vigorous combustion of magnesium in pure oxygen
Recognise the formation of a metal oxide
Learn the eye-protection measure required when observing high-intensity light

sulfur-oxygen-blue-flame.title: Combustion of Sulfur Powder in Oxygen
sulfur-oxygen-blue-flame.description: Sulfur powder burning in air produces only a pale blue flame, but when introduced into pure oxygen the flame becomes a bright blue-violet; the product is sulfur dioxide, which has a pungent, irritating odour.
objectives: Compare the flame colour of sulfur burning in air versus in pure oxygen
Recognise the irritating properties of sulfur dioxide
Learn how to absorb toxic gases using an alkaline solution

iron-wire-oxygen-sparks.title: Iron Wire Burning in Oxygen with Vigorous Sparking
iron-wire-oxygen-sparks.description: A coiled iron wire with a match head tied to its tip is ignited and lowered into a gas collection bottle of oxygen; the wire burns vigorously with intense sparking and produces black iron(II,III) oxide, so a layer of fine sand must be placed at the bottom of the bottle.
objectives: Observe the vigorous combustion of iron wire in pure oxygen
Understand the effect of oxygen concentration on combustion intensity
Learn the procedure of placing sand at the bottom of the bottle to prevent it from cracking

charcoal-oxygen-white-glow.title: Combustion of Charcoal in Oxygen
charcoal-oxygen-white-glow.description: Red-hot charcoal introduced into oxygen glows with a white light; after combustion, limewater poured into the bottle turns cloudy when shaken, confirming that carbon dioxide is the combustion product.
objectives: Observe the white glow produced when charcoal burns in pure oxygen
Test for carbon dioxide as the combustion product
Compare the observed phenomena in air and in pure oxygen

hydrogen-oxygen-quiet-flame.title: Quiet Combustion of Hydrogen Gas in Oxygen
hydrogen-oxygen-quiet-flame.description: Hydrogen gas, after being tested for purity, burns quietly in oxygen with a pale blue flame; when a cold, dry beaker is held over the flame, water droplets condense on its inner surface.
objectives: Observe the pale blue flame of burning hydrogen gas
Confirm that water is the combustion product from the condensed droplets
Emphasise that hydrogen gas must be tested for purity before ignition

hydrogen-reduce-fe2o3.title: Reduction of Iron(III) Oxide by Hydrogen Gas
hydrogen-reduce-fe2o3.description: Dry hydrogen gas is passed over heated iron(III) oxide; the reddish-brown solid gradually turns black and water droplets appear at the mouth of the tube. The correct procedure requires that gas flow must be established before the burner is lit.
objectives: Verify the reducing property of hydrogen gas
Observe the colour change as iron(III) oxide is reduced
Master the correct operating sequence to prevent explosion

co-reduce-cuo-tail-gas.title: Reduction of Copper(II) Oxide by Carbon Monoxide and Tail-Gas Treatment
co-reduce-cuo-tail-gas.description: Carbon monoxide is passed over heated copper(II) oxide; the black solid turns brick-red and the tail gas must be either ignited or collected — direct release into the atmosphere is strictly prohibited, making this a classic case study in tail-gas treatment.
objectives: Verify the reducing property of carbon monoxide
Test for carbon dioxide among the reaction products
Understand why toxic tail gases must be treated before release
