chlorine-naoh-bleach-liquid.title: Preparation of Bleaching Solution from Chlorine and Sodium Hydroxide
chlorine-naoh-bleach-liquid.description: When yellow-green chlorine is passed into sodium hydroxide solution, the colour disappears rapidly as sodium hypochlorite bleaching solution forms; this reaction also serves as the standard method for absorbing chlorine tail gas.
objectives: Observe the decolourisation of yellow-green chlorine as it is absorbed by an alkali
Understand the bleaching action of hypochlorite salts
Learn the standard method for absorbing chlorine tail gas

chlorine-lime-bleaching-powder.title: Preparation of Bleaching Powder from Chlorine and Lime Milk
chlorine-lime-bleaching-powder.description: When chlorine is passed into lime milk, the yellow-green colour disappears as the turbid suspension absorbs the gas, yielding bleaching powder whose active constituent is calcium hypochlorite.
objectives: Understand the principle behind the industrial preparation of bleaching powder
Recognise calcium hypochlorite as the active constituent of bleaching powder
Explain why bleaching powder must be stored in a sealed container

ammonia-water-fountain.title: Fountain Experiment Demonstrating the Solubility of Ammonia Gas in Water
ammonia-water-fountain.description: When water is introduced into a round-bottom flask filled with ammonia gas, the extremely rapid dissolution of ammonia causes a sharp drop in pressure inside the flask; atmospheric pressure then forces water upward to produce a fountain, which turns red upon addition of phenolphthalein.
objectives: Understand the pressure principle underlying the fountain experiment
Verify the alkaline nature of aqueous ammonia
Recognise the exceptionally high solubility of ammonia gas in water

ammonia-hcl-white-smoke.title: Formation of White Smoke from Ammonia Gas and Hydrogen Chloride
ammonia-hcl-white-smoke.description: When two glass stirring rods, one dipped in concentrated aqueous ammonia and the other in concentrated hydrochloric acid, are brought close together, a dense white smoke of ammonium chloride immediately forms in the air between them; this is the classic mutual-detection reaction for these two gases.
objectives: Observe the formation of a solid white smoke through a gas-phase reaction
Learn the mutual-detection method for ammonia gas and hydrogen chloride
Distinguish between the concepts of white smoke and white mist

copper-air-heating-black.title: Blackening of Copper upon Heating in Air
copper-air-heating-black.description: When a copper strip is heated over an alcohol lamp, its surface gradually turns black as copper(II) oxide forms; subsequent exposure to hydrogen gas restores the original red colour, completing an oxidation–reduction cycle.
objectives: Observe the colour change resulting from the oxidation of copper by oxygen
Recognise the two oxide forms corresponding to the two oxidation states of copper
Prepare for the follow-up oxidation–reduction cycle experiment

ethanol-oxygen-combustion.title: Complete Combustion of Ethanol in Oxygen
ethanol-oxygen-combustion.description: Ethanol burns in an adequate supply of oxygen with a pale-blue flame, producing carbon dioxide and water; the high flame temperature and absence of black smoke make ethanol a typical example of a clean fuel.
objectives: Observe the flame produced by the complete combustion of ethanol
Identify the products of combustion
Compare the phenomena of complete combustion and incomplete combustion

sodium-oxygen-peroxide.title: Combustion of Sodium in Oxygen to Form Sodium Peroxide
sodium-oxygen-peroxide.description: Sodium metal oxidises slowly in air to give white sodium oxide, but when heated and ignited it burns with a yellow flame to produce pale-yellow sodium peroxide, demonstrating that reaction conditions determine the product.
objectives: Understand how reaction conditions influence the product formed
Observe the yellow flame produced by burning sodium
Learn the correct handling and storage procedures for reactive metals

sodium-sulfide-acid-h2s.title: Generation of Hydrogen Sulfide from Sodium Sulfide and Acid
sodium-sulfide-acid-h2s.description: Adding dilute sulfuric acid to solid sodium sulfide releases hydrogen sulfide gas with a characteristic rotten-egg odour; when the gas is passed into copper(II) sulfate solution, a black precipitate forms. This experiment must be carried out in a fume cupboard.
objectives: Learn the laboratory preparation of hydrogen sulfide
Use a heavy-metal salt solution to detect hydrogen sulfide
Implement proper ventilation and absorption measures when working with toxic gases

bisulfite-acid-so2.title: Preparation of Sulfur Dioxide from Sodium Bisulfite and Acid
bisulfite-acid-so2.description: Sodium bisulfite reacts rapidly with dilute sulfuric acid to release sulfur dioxide with evolution of heat. The gas decolorizes fuchsin solution, and the color is restored upon heating.
objectives: Master a convenient laboratory method for preparing sulfur dioxide
Verify the reversibility of sulfur dioxide bleaching
Master the absorption of tail gas using an alkaline solution

iron-sulfide-acid-h2s.title: Preparation of Hydrogen Sulfide from Iron(II) Sulfide and Acid
iron-sulfide-acid-h2s.description: Lump iron(II) sulfide reacts with dilute sulfuric acid in a Kipp's generator, allowing smooth control over the generation and cessation of hydrogen sulfide. This serves as a model demonstration of on-demand gas preparation.
objectives: Master the conditions under which a Kipp's generator is applicable
Understand why lump solids allow on-demand start and stop of gas generation
Implement safe handling procedures for hydrogen sulfide

ammonia-nitric-acid-smoke.title: Formation of Ammonium Nitrate White Fumes from Ammonia Gas and Nitric Acid
ammonia-nitric-acid-smoke.description: Vapors from concentrated aqueous ammonia and concentrated nitric acid combine to produce white fumes of ammonium nitrate. The reaction is exothermic and serves as a small-scale demonstration of industrial ammonium nitrate fertilizer synthesis.
objectives: Observe the fume-forming reaction between a volatile acid and ammonia gas
Connect the demonstration to the industrial synthesis of ammonium nitrate fertilizer
Understand that white fumes consist of suspended microscopic crystals

co2-baoh2-precipitate.title: Passing Carbon Dioxide into Barium Hydroxide Solution
co2-baoh2-precipitate.description: Carbon dioxide passed into barium hydroxide solution produces a white barium carbonate precipitate, giving a more sensitive test than limewater. Continued addition of excess gas causes the precipitate to redissolve.
objectives: Compare the sensitivity of barium hydroxide solution and limewater as tests for carbon dioxide
Observe the formation and subsequent dissolution of the precipitate
Write the chemical equation for the reaction with excess carbon dioxide

co2-koh-pressure-drop.title: Collapse of a Soft Plastic Bottle Caused by Absorption of Carbon Dioxide by Potassium Hydroxide
co2-koh-pressure-drop.description: A soft plastic bottle filled with carbon dioxide is injected with potassium hydroxide solution, sealed, and shaken. Absorption of the gas causes a sharp drop in internal pressure, and the bottle collapses visibly.
objectives: Use the change in pressure to demonstrate that the gas has been absorbed
Compare the extent to which carbon dioxide dissolves in water versus in an alkaline solution
Design a controlled experiment to rule out the effect of dissolution in water alone

bicarbonate-acetic-fizz.title: Gas Evolution from Sodium Bicarbonate and Acetic Acid
bicarbonate-acetic-fizz.description: Household baking soda mixed with table vinegar produces vigorous effervescence immediately. This is the most accessible gas-evolution reaction in a kitchen setting and can be used to estimate the purity of the baking soda.
objectives: Observe gas evolution from the reaction of a weak acid with a bicarbonate
Connect the reaction to the practical use of baking powder
Estimate the sodium bicarbonate content from the volume of gas produced

ammonium-chloride-lime-ammonia.title: Preparation of Ammonia Gas by Heating Ammonium Chloride with Slaked Lime
ammonium-chloride-lime-ammonia.description: A mixture of ammonium chloride and slaked lime is heated to release ammonia gas. The reaction is endothermic and requires sustained heating. This is the standard laboratory method for preparing ammonia gas.
objectives: Master the laboratory preparation of ammonia gas
Understand why ammonia gas is collected by upward displacement of air
Master the methods for testing and drying ammonia gas

lead-iodide-golden-rain.title: Golden Rain of Lead(II) Iodide
lead-iodide-golden-rain.description: Mixing lead(II) nitrate solution with potassium iodide solution immediately produces a bright yellow precipitate of lead(II) iodide. On heating, the precipitate dissolves, and slow cooling allows recrystallization to yield glistening golden hexagonal platelets.
objectives: Observe the formation of bright yellow lead(II) iodide
Understand how recrystallization results from the temperature dependence of solubility
Compare the appearance of an amorphous precipitate with that of well-formed crystals

silver-carbonate-precipitate.title: Formation and Decomposition of Silver Carbonate Precipitate
silver-carbonate-precipitate.description: Silver nitrate reacts with sodium carbonate to form a white silver carbonate precipitate, which gradually darkens on heating or exposure to light, demonstrating the general instability of silver salts.
objectives: Observe the formation of silver carbonate
Recognise the instability of silver salts
Write the ionic equation for the formation of silver carbonate

barium-carbonate-vs-sulfate.title: Comparison of Acid Solubility: Barium Carbonate versus Barium Sulfate
barium-carbonate-vs-sulfate.description: Sodium carbonate and sodium sulfate are reacted separately with barium nitrate to produce two white precipitates; on addition of dilute nitric acid, barium carbonate dissolves with effervescence whereas barium sulfate remains undissolved, enabling the two to be distinguished.
objectives: Prepare two white barium salt precipitates
Use acid solubility to distinguish carbonates from sulfates
Understand why carbonate ions must be excluded before testing for sulfate ions

barium-sulfite-precipitate.title: Formation and Oxidation of Barium Sulfite Precipitate
barium-sulfite-precipitate.description: Barium chloride reacts with sodium sulfite to give a white barium sulfite precipitate; subsequent treatment with hydrogen peroxide oxidises the precipitate to barium sulfate, which is insoluble in acid, providing evidence for the change in oxidation state of sulfur.
objectives: Prepare a barium sulfite precipitate
Observe the change in acid solubility after the precipitate is oxidised
Understand the criteria for precipitate transformation

zinc-hydroxide-amphoteric.title: Amphoteric Dissolution of Zinc Hydroxide
zinc-hydroxide-amphoteric.description: Addition of a small amount of sodium hydroxide to zinc sulfate solution produces a white zinc hydroxide precipitate; further addition of excess alkali causes the precipitate to redissolve, exhibiting amphoteric behaviour analogous to that of aluminium.
objectives: Observe the initial formation and subsequent dissolution of the precipitate
Recognise the amphoteric nature of zinc hydroxide
Compare the properties of the hydroxides of zinc and aluminium

cobalt-hydroxide-pink.title: Pink Precipitate of Cobalt(II) Hydroxide
cobalt-hydroxide-pink.description: Addition of sodium hydroxide to a cobalt(II) chloride solution produces a pink cobalt(II) hydroxide precipitate, which turns dark brown on prolonged standing owing to oxidation by atmospheric oxygen, illustrating the variable oxidation states of cobalt.
objectives: Observe the formation of the pink cobalt(II) hydroxide precipitate
Recognise the characteristic colours of transition-metal hydroxides
Understand the colour change caused by oxidation in air

nickel-hydroxide-green.title: Apple-Green Precipitate of Nickel(II) Hydroxide
nickel-hydroxide-green.description: Addition of alkali to a nickel(II) chloride solution produces an apple-green nickel(II) hydroxide precipitate, which is an important qualitative indicator for nickel ions and is also used as the positive-electrode material in nickel–metal hydride batteries.
objectives: Observe the formation of the apple-green precipitate
Master the qualitative identification of nickel ions
Make connections to the electrode materials used in nickel–metal hydride batteries

copper-sulfide-black.title: Black Precipitate of Copper(II) Sulfide
copper-sulfide-black.description: Addition of sodium sulfide to copper(II) sulfate solution immediately produces a black copper(II) sulfide precipitate of extremely low solubility that does not dissolve even on addition of dilute hydrochloric acid, demonstrating its very small solubility product.
objectives: Observe the formation of the black copper(II) sulfide precipitate
Understand why precipitates with very small solubility products do not dissolve in strong acids
Master the use of sulfide precipitation to remove heavy-metal ions

silver-sulfide-tarnish.title: Silver Sulfide and the Tarnishing of Silverware
silver-sulfide-tarnish.description: Silver nitrate reacts with sodium sulfide to produce a black silver sulfide precipitate, which is the chemical reason why silver jewellery darkens on prolonged contact with sulfur-containing substances; the tarnish can be reversed by treating the object with aluminium foil and brine.
objectives: Observe the formation of the black silver sulfide precipitate
Explain the chemical cause of tarnishing in silverware
Design an electrochemical cleaning procedure using aluminium foil

lead-sulfide-detection.title: Detection of Lead Ions via Lead(II) Sulfide Precipitation
lead-sulfide-detection.description: Adding sodium sulfide to lead-containing wastewater produces a black lead(II) sulfide precipitate. The reaction is highly sensitive and represents a standard precipitation method for treating heavy-metal wastewater.
objectives: Master the sulfide-based test for lead ions
Understand the sulfide precipitation method for treating heavy-metal wastewater
Recognize the environmental hazards of lead contamination

calcium-fluoride-precipitate.title: Calcium Fluoride Precipitation and Treatment of Fluoride-Containing Wastewater
calcium-fluoride-precipitate.description: Adding calcium chloride to a sodium fluoride solution produces a white calcium fluoride precipitate. This reaction is the basis of the standard lime process for treating industrial fluoride-containing wastewater, and calcium fluoride is also the principal component of the mineral fluorite.
objectives: Observe the formation of calcium fluoride
Understand the chemical principles of the lime defluoridation process
Connect the reaction product to the composition of fluorite

calcium-phosphate-bone.title: Calcium Phosphate Precipitation and the Composition of Bone
calcium-phosphate-bone.description: Mixing sodium phosphate with calcium chloride produces a white calcium phosphate precipitate, which is the principal inorganic component of bones and teeth and a raw material for superphosphate fertilizer.
objectives: Observe the formation of calcium phosphate
Recognize its biological role in the human body
Verify that calcium phosphate dissolves in strong acids

silver-phosphate-yellow.title: The Yellow Precipitate of Silver Phosphate
silver-phosphate-yellow.description: Adding silver nitrate to a sodium phosphate solution produces a yellow silver phosphate precipitate that dissolves in dilute nitric acid. This behavior is a key distinction between phosphate ions and halide ions.
objectives: Observe the formation of the yellow silver phosphate precipitate
Use nitric acid to distinguish silver phosphate from silver halides
Master the qualitative test for phosphate ions

magnesium-carbonate-precipitate.title: Magnesium Carbonate Precipitation and the Concentration of Magnesium
magnesium-carbonate-precipitate.description: Adding sodium carbonate to a magnesium sulfate solution produces a white magnesium carbonate precipitate. Calcination of this precipitate yields magnesium oxide, which is one of the key steps in extracting magnesium from brine.
objectives: Observe the formation of magnesium carbonate
Understand how the precipitation method is used to concentrate magnesium
Master the sequential operations of filtration and calcination

zinc-sulfide-white.title: The White Precipitate of Zinc Sulfide
zinc-sulfide-white.description: Mixing zinc sulfate with sodium sulfide produces a white zinc sulfide precipitate, which contrasts sharply with the dark colors of other heavy-metal sulfides and can be used for group separation of cations.
objectives: Observe the formation of the white zinc sulfide precipitate
Compare the colors of different metal sulfide precipitates
Understand the analytical rationale behind group precipitation of sulfides

calcium-sulfite-flue-gas.title: Calcium Sulfite Precipitation and Flue-Gas Desulfurization
calcium-sulfite-flue-gas.description: Mixing calcium chloride with sodium sulfite produces a white calcium sulfite precipitate, modeling the salt-forming step of the lime-based flue-gas desulfurization process. Oxidation of the product yields gypsum.
objectives: Observe the formation of calcium sulfite
Understand the chemical principles of the lime desulfurization process
Recognize the resource recovery potential of desulfurization gypsum

lead-sulfate-white.title: The White Precipitate of Lead(II) Sulfate
lead-sulfate-white.description: Mixing lead(II) nitrate with sodium sulfate produces a white lead(II) sulfate precipitate. During discharge of a lead–acid battery, this compound deposits on both electrodes and is the direct cause of battery degradation.
objectives: Observe the formation of lead(II) sulfate
Connect the precipitate to the discharge products of a lead–acid battery
Understand how sulfation leads to a decline in battery capacity

barium-phosphate-precipitate.title: Barium Phosphate Precipitation and Phosphorus Removal
barium-phosphate-precipitate.description: Sodium phosphate reacts with barium chloride to form a white precipitate of barium phosphate. This reaction can be applied in quantitative studies of phosphorus removal from water bodies to inhibit eutrophication.
objectives: Observe the formation of barium phosphate precipitate
Understand the principle of chemical phosphorus removal
Connect the reaction to the treatment of aquatic eutrophication

iron-carbonate-precipitate.title: Formation and Oxidation of Iron(II) Carbonate Precipitate
iron-carbonate-precipitate.description: Iron(II) sulfate reacts with sodium carbonate to form a white precipitate of iron(II) carbonate, which rapidly turns yellow-brown in air, demonstrating that Fe²⁺ is readily oxidised.
objectives: Observe the formation and colour change of iron(II) carbonate precipitate
Understand the tendency of iron(II) ions to undergo oxidation
Learn the rationale for preparing iron(II) compounds under air-free conditions

basic-copper-carbonate-patina.title: Basic Copper Carbonate and Patina
basic-copper-carbonate-patina.description: Copper(II) sulfate reacts with sodium carbonate solution to produce green basic copper carbonate, the principal constituent of patina on copper artefacts; on heating it decomposes to black copper(II) oxide.
objectives: Observe the formation of green basic copper carbonate
Explain the origin of patina on copper surfaces
Observe the thermal decomposition of basic copper carbonate to black copper(II) oxide

silver-sulfate-slightly-soluble.title: Slight Solubility of Silver Sulfate
silver-sulfate-slightly-soluble.description: A white precipitate of silver sulfate forms only when concentrated silver nitrate solution meets relatively concentrated sodium sulfate solution; no precipitate appears in dilute solutions, illustrating concretely that «slightly soluble» lies between «soluble» and «insoluble.»
objectives: Understand the concentration dependence of slightly soluble substances
Compare the observable phenomena under dilute and concentrated conditions
Use the solubility product to predict whether a precipitate will form

lead-chloride-hot-water.title: Dissolution of Lead Chloride in Hot Water
lead-chloride-hot-water.description: Lead(II) nitrate reacts with sodium chloride to form a white precipitate of lead chloride, which dissolves on heating and recrystallises as fine needles on cooling, serving as a classic example of strong temperature dependence of solubility.
objectives: Observe the dissolution of the precipitate on heating and its reappearance on cooling
Understand the temperature dependence of solubility
Compare the solubility of lead chloride with that of silver chloride

mno2-concentrated-hcl-chlorine.title: Preparation of Chlorine from Manganese(IV) Oxide and Concentrated Hydrochloric Acid
mno2-concentrated-hcl-chlorine.description: Heating a mixture of manganese(IV) oxide and concentrated hydrochloric acid produces yellow-green chlorine gas, illustrating that concentration is a decisive factor in determining whether a redox reaction will proceed.
objectives: Master the principle and apparatus for the laboratory preparation of chlorine
Understand why dilute hydrochloric acid cannot be oxidised by manganese(IV) oxide
Learn to absorb chlorine tail gas with alkali solution

kmno4-concentrated-hcl-chlorine.title: Room-Temperature Preparation of Chlorine from Potassium Permanganate and Concentrated Hydrochloric Acid
kmno4-concentrated-hcl-chlorine.description: Potassium permanganate is a far stronger oxidising agent than manganese(IV) oxide; adding concentrated hydrochloric acid at room temperature releases chlorine immediately without heating, providing a useful contrast with the manganese(IV) oxide method.
objectives: Compare the oxidising strengths of potassium permanganate and manganese(IV) oxide
Master a procedure for preparing chlorine without heating
Handle toxic tail gas safely and in accordance with laboratory regulations

kclo3-mno2-oxygen.title: Catalytic Decomposition of Potassium Chlorate to Produce Oxygen
kclo3-mno2-oxygen.description: Heating a mixture of potassium chlorate with a small amount of manganese(IV) oxide releases oxygen rapidly; a glowing wooden splint relights, demonstrating that a catalyst alters the reaction conditions without itself becoming part of the products.
objectives: Master the principle of preparing oxygen from potassium chlorate
Understand the definition and characteristics of a catalyst
Learn to collect oxygen by water displacement and to verify that the collection vessel is full

iron-burning-chlorine.title: Combustion of Iron Wire in Chlorine to Form Iron(III) Chloride
iron-burning-chlorine.description: When a heated iron wire is inserted into a jar of chlorine, it burns vigorously, producing brown fumes. The product is iron(III) chloride rather than iron(II) chloride, demonstrating that chlorine oxidizes iron to its highest oxidation state.
objectives: Observe the brown fumes produced when iron wire burns in chlorine
Understand how the strength of an oxidizing agent determines the oxidation state of the product
Compare this reaction with the reaction of iron and hydrochloric acid, which yields only iron(II) salts

copper-burning-chlorine.title: Combustion of Copper Wire in Chlorine
copper-burning-chlorine.description: When copper wire burns in chlorine, brown-yellow fumes are produced; dissolving the product in water yields a blue-green copper(II) chloride solution, providing direct evidence of chlorine's strong oxidizing power.
objectives: Observe the combustion of copper wire in chlorine
Understand that chlorine can directly oxidize less reactive metals
Recognize the characteristic color of a copper(II) chloride solution

hydrogen-burning-chlorine.title: Combustion of Hydrogen Gas in Chlorine
hydrogen-burning-chlorine.description: Hydrogen gas burns quietly in chlorine with a pale blue flame, and white mist appears at the mouth of the collection vessel; this reaction is the basis of the industrial synthesis of hydrochloric acid.
objectives: Observe the pale blue flame and the white mist at the vessel opening
Understand the explosion hazard when this reaction is initiated by light
Connect the laboratory reaction to the industrial process for synthesizing hydrochloric acid

sodium-burning-chlorine.title: Combustion of Sodium in Chlorine to Form Table Salt (Sodium Chloride)
sodium-burning-chlorine.description: Molten sodium burns vigorously in chlorine with a yellow flame, generating dense white smoke composed of minute crystals of table salt (sodium chloride).
objectives: Observe the yellow flame and white smoke when sodium burns in chlorine
Understand that ionic compounds can form directly from their constituent elements
Follow safe-handling procedures for reactive metals

zinc-concentrated-sulfuric-so2.title: Reaction of Zinc Granules with Concentrated Sulfuric Acid to Produce Sulfur Dioxide
zinc-concentrated-sulfuric-so2.description: When zinc granules are added to concentrated sulfuric acid and the mixture is heated, the gas evolved is sulfur dioxide with a pungent odor rather than hydrogen gas, showing that the oxidizing action of concentrated sulfuric acid is due to the sulfur atom gaining electrons.
objectives: Compare the gases produced when zinc granules react with dilute versus concentrated sulfuric acid
Understand that the oxidizing property of concentrated sulfuric acid originates from S(+6)
Learn to absorb sulfur dioxide using an alkaline solution

zinc-dilute-sulfuric-hydrogen.title: Reaction of Zinc Granules with Dilute Sulfuric Acid to Produce Hydrogen Gas
zinc-dilute-sulfuric-hydrogen.description: The same zinc granules added to dilute sulfuric acid evolve only colorless, odorless hydrogen gas, forming a controlled contrast with the concentrated sulfuric acid experiment and highlighting how concentration can fundamentally alter the nature of a reaction.
objectives: Observe the production of hydrogen gas when zinc granules react with dilute sulfuric acid
Confirm the identity of hydrogen gas by ignition
Understand the fundamental difference in oxidizing behavior between concentrated and dilute sulfuric acid

zinc-concentrated-nitric-no2.title: Reaction of Zinc Granules with Concentrated Nitric Acid to Produce Red-Brown Nitrogen Dioxide
zinc-concentrated-nitric-no2.description: Zinc granules react vigorously with concentrated nitric acid, releasing red-brown nitrogen dioxide; the distinctive color of the gas itself serves as direct evidence for identifying the product.
objectives: Observe the formation of red-brown nitrogen dioxide
Understand that the reduction product of concentrated nitric acid is NO₂
Learn procedures for absorbing nitrogen-containing tail gases

zinc-dilute-nitric-no.title: Reaction of Zinc Granules with Dilute Nitric Acid to Produce Colorless Nitric Oxide
zinc-dilute-nitric-no.description: Dilute nitric acid reacts with zinc to produce colorless nitric oxide, which immediately turns red-brown upon contact with air at the mouth of the delivery tube — the classic method for identifying NO.
objectives: Observe the color change of NO to red-brown as it exits the delivery tube into air
Understand that the reduction product of dilute nitric acid is NO
Learn to collect water-insoluble NO by the displacement of water method

iron-concentrated-nitric-no2.title: Vigorous Reaction of Iron with Concentrated Nitric Acid
iron-concentrated-nitric-no2.description: At room temperature, iron undergoes passivation in concentrated nitric acid; upon heating, the reaction becomes vigorous and releases reddish-brown nitrogen dioxide, illustrating both the protective effect of the passive film and its eventual breakdown.
objectives: Recognise the passivation of iron in concentrated nitric acid
Observe the formation of NO₂ after heating
Understand the application of passivation in industrial storage and transport

fe3-oxidize-sulfide-sulfur.title: Oxidation of Sulfide Ion by Iron(III) to Precipitate Sulfur
fe3-oxidize-sulfide-sulfur.description: When iron(III) chloride solution is added to sodium sulfide solution, no iron(III) sulfide precipitate forms; instead, pale yellow elemental sulfur is deposited and the solution turns light green, demonstrating that Fe³⁺ has a greater oxidising power than S.
objectives: Observe the deposition of pale yellow sulfur
Understand why redox reaction takes precedence over double decomposition
Establish the experimental criterion for comparing oxidising power

hypochlorite-iodide-oxidation.title: Oxidation of Iodide Ion by Hypochlorite
hypochlorite-iodide-oxidation.description: When household bleach is added to a starch–potassium iodide solution, an immediate blue colour develops, confirming that hypochlorite is a strong oxidising agent and providing the chemical basis for its disinfecting action.
objectives: Observe the blue colour of starch as an indicator of iodine formation
Understand the oxidising property of hypochlorite
Connect the result to the mechanism of action of everyday disinfectants

iodine-thiosulfate-endpoint.title: End-Point Determination in Iodometric Titration with Sodium Thiosulfate
iodine-thiosulfate-endpoint.description: In the titration of an iodine–starch solution with sodium thiosulfate, the end point is reached when the blue colour just disappears and does not return within half a minute, representing a classical procedure in quantitative analysis.
objectives: Master end-point recognition in iodometric titration
Understand the quantitative reducing action of sodium thiosulfate
Practise correct burette reading and handling technique

methane-oxygen-combustion.title: Combustion of Methane in Oxygen
methane-oxygen-combustion.description: Methane burns in oxygen with a pale blue flame; holding a dry, cold beaker above the flame produces water droplets, and passing the combustion gases into limewater turns it milky, confirming that the products contain both hydrogen and carbon.
objectives: Observe the pale blue flame of burning methane
Use a two-step test to confirm that the products are CO₂ and H₂O
Understand the general equation for complete combustion of a hydrocarbon

carbon-monoxide-burning.title: Blue Flame of Carbon Monoxide Combustion
carbon-monoxide-burning.description: Pure carbon monoxide burns with a pale blue flame, which is the principal heat-releasing reaction in coal gas combustion; the experiment also serves as a reminder that carbon monoxide is highly toxic and that any leakage must be strictly prevented.
objectives: Observe the pale blue flame produced by burning carbon monoxide
Verify that carbon dioxide is the combustion product
Understand the mechanism of carbon monoxide poisoning and relevant safety precautions

red-phosphorus-oxygen-smoke.title: Combustion of Red Phosphorus in Oxygen Producing White Smoke
red-phosphorus-oxygen-smoke.description: Red phosphorus burns in oxygen with a yellow flame and generates dense white smoke; the product, phosphorus pentoxide, is highly hygroscopic, and this reaction can be used to determine the volume fraction of oxygen in air.
objectives: Observe the yellow flame and white smoke produced by burning red phosphorus
Recognise the hygroscopic nature of phosphorus pentoxide
Understand the experimental design for determining the oxygen content of air

zinc-oxygen-blue-green.title: Combustion of Zinc Powder in Oxygen
zinc-oxygen-blue-green.description: Zinc powder burns in oxygen with a blue-green light and yields a white powder of zinc oxide; zinc oxide is widely used as a raw material in sunscreens and pigments.
objectives: Observe the blue-green light emitted during the combustion of zinc
Recognise the appearance and uses of zinc oxide
Compare the flame colours produced by the combustion of different metals

dichromate-sulfite-green.title: Oxidation of Sulfite by Potassium Dichromate
dichromate-sulfite-green.description: In acidic solution, potassium dichromate rapidly oxidises sodium sulfite, and the characteristic orange-yellow colour changes to the green of chromium(III), illustrating the reduction of hexavalent chromium and the chemical basis of industrial wastewater detoxification.
objectives: Observe the colour change from orange-yellow to green
Understand the reductive detoxification of hexavalent chromium
Recognise how acidic conditions enhance oxidising power

h2o2-oxidize-fe2.title: Oxidation of Iron(II) by Hydrogen Peroxide
h2o2-oxidize-fe2.description: When hydrogen peroxide is added dropwise to a pale-green iron(II) sulfate solution, the colour shifts to brown-yellow; subsequent addition of potassium thiocyanate produces an immediate blood-red coloration, confirming the formation of iron(III).
objectives: Observe the colour change accompanying the oxidation of iron(II)
Use potassium thiocyanate to confirm the formation of iron(III)
Understand the environmentally benign character of hydrogen peroxide as an oxidising agent

sulfite-reduce-fe3.title: Reduction of Iron(III) by Sulfite
sulfite-reduce-fe3.description: Adding sodium sulfite dropwise to a brown-yellow iron(III) chloride solution causes the colour to fade to pale green as sulfate is produced, forming a complementary pair with the preceding hydrogen peroxide experiment and illustrating the reversible interconversion of the two oxidation states of iron.
objectives: Observe the oxidation-state change as brown-yellow fades to pale green
Recognise sodium sulfite as a reducing agent
Compare how the two oxidation states of iron interconvert

sodium-peroxide-water-oxygen.title: Reaction of Sodium Peroxide with Water to Generate Oxygen
sodium-peroxide-water-oxygen.description: When pale-yellow sodium peroxide is added to water, the reaction is strongly exothermic and releases oxygen; a glowing wooden splint reignites, and a drop of phenolphthalein turns red before fading, demonstrating the principle behind sodium peroxide as an oxygen-supplying agent.
objectives: Observe the release of oxygen when sodium peroxide reacts with water
Distinguish this reaction from those of sodium and sodium oxide with respect to gas evolution
Understand why phenolphthalein first turns red and then decolourises

sodium-peroxide-co2-air-regeneration.title: Absorption of Carbon Dioxide by Sodium Peroxide with Oxygen Release
sodium-peroxide-co2-air-regeneration.description: When carbon dioxide is passed through sodium peroxide, the pale-yellow solid turns white and oxygen is released; the volume ratio of gas absorbed to gas released is 2∶1, which is precisely the basis of air-regeneration systems in sealed cabins.
objectives: Observe the solid change from pale yellow to white with concurrent oxygen release
Understand how the 2∶1 volume ratio matches the demands of respiratory gas exchange
Appreciate the oxygen-supply design used in submarines and spacecraft

sodium-oxide-water-base.title: Reaction of Sodium Oxide with Water to Form a Base
sodium-oxide-water-base.description: Sodium oxide combines directly with water to form sodium hydroxide, releasing heat but no gas; the strict contrast with sodium peroxide highlights the difference in oxygen oxidation state between the two compounds.
objectives: Observe the combination of a basic oxide with water
Compare the gas-releasing behaviour of sodium peroxide with the gas-free reaction of sodium oxide
Understand how the oxidation state of oxygen determines the type of reaction

alumina-strong-base-dissolve.title: Dissolution of Aluminium Oxide in Strong Base as Evidence of Amphoteric Character
alumina-strong-base-dissolve.description: White aluminium oxide powder dissolves in both dilute sulfuric acid and sodium hydroxide solution; both test tubes clear simultaneously, providing the most complete criterion for classifying a substance as an amphoteric oxide.
objectives: Observe the dissolution of aluminium oxide in both acidic and basic solution
Master the criteria for identifying an amphoteric oxide
Understand the formation of aluminate salts

zinc-oxide-amphoteric-both.title: Amphoteric Dissolution of Zinc Oxide in Both Acid and Base
zinc-oxide-amphoteric-both.description: Zinc oxide dissolves to give a clear solution when added separately to hydrochloric acid and to sodium hydroxide, demonstrating that it belongs, alongside aluminium oxide, to the class of amphoteric oxides; it is also the active ingredient in sunscreen formulations.
objectives: Verify the amphoteric character of zinc oxide
Compare the positions of zinc and aluminium in the periodic table
Appreciate the practical applications of zinc oxide in everyday products

thermite-iron-oxide-weld.title: Thermite Reduction of Iron(III) Oxide
thermite-iron-oxide-weld.description: Igniting a mixture of aluminium powder and iron(III) oxide with magnesium ribbon (for ignition) produces an intensely bright white flash; the molten iron runs down and solidifies into metal beads, demonstrating the field-welding method used for railway tracks.
objectives: Observe the extreme temperature and molten metal produced in the thermite reaction
Understand the origin of aluminium's strong reducing power
Recognise the industrial application of thermite welding

thermite-copper-oxide.title: Thermite Reaction: Aluminium Powder Reducing Copper(II) Oxide
thermite-copper-oxide.description: Igniting a mixture of aluminium powder and black copper(II) oxide causes vigorous exothermic reaction and deposits reddish copper, providing a vivid demonstration that aluminium is far more reactive than copper.
objectives: Observe the reduction of black copper(II) oxide to reddish copper
Compare the reducing power of aluminium and copper
Practise the ignition procedure and safety precautions for thermite reactions

magnetite-acid-dissolve.title: Dissolving Iron(II,III) Oxide in Hydrochloric Acid
magnetite-acid-dissolve.description: Black magnetic iron(II,III) oxide dissolves in hydrochloric acid to yield a mixed solution containing both iron(II) and iron(III) ions, which are then detected separately using potassium thiocyanate and potassium hexacyanoferrate(III).
objectives: Observe the dissolution of magnetic iron(II,III) oxide
Understand that Fe₃O₄ contains iron in two oxidation states
Master the individual detection tests for iron(II) and iron(III) ions

iron-hydroxide-acid-dissolve.title: Dissolving Iron(III) Hydroxide in Acid to Regenerate an Iron Salt
iron-hydroxide-acid-dissolve.description: Adding sulfuric acid to a reddish-brown iron(III) hydroxide precipitate dissolves it to give a yellow-brown solution, illustrating the interconversion between precipitates and salts as one step in the iron cycle.
objectives: Observe the reddish-brown precipitate dissolving to give a yellow-brown solution
Understand the interconversion of precipitates and salts
Establish the general pattern for reactions of insoluble bases with acids

copper-hydroxide-acid-blue.title: Dissolving Copper(II) Hydroxide in Hydrochloric Acid
copper-hydroxide-acid-blue.description: The blue copper(II) hydroxide precipitate dissolves rapidly in hydrochloric acid to form a blue-green copper(II) chloride solution; the gradual change in colour depth serves as a visual indicator of reaction progress.
objectives: Observe the dissolution of the blue precipitate
Compare the colours of the solutions obtained after dissolving copper(II) hydroxide and iron(III) hydroxide
Practise the acid-dissolution procedure for insoluble bases

lead-silver-nitrate-tree.title: Displacement of Silver by Lead — the «Silver Tree»
lead-silver-nitrate-tree.description: A lead strip immersed in silver nitrate solution slowly develops a coating of silvery, dendrite-shaped crystals on its surface, producing one of the most visually striking examples of a displacement reaction.
objectives: Observe the growth of dendritic silver crystals
Confirm that lead is more reactive than silver
Understand the phenomenon of preferential crystal growth along defect sites

zinc-copper-chloride-displacement.title: Displacement of Copper from Copper(II) Chloride by Zinc
zinc-copper-chloride-displacement.description: Zinc granules placed in blue-green copper(II) chloride solution become coated with a layer of reddish copper while the solution gradually loses colour, providing direct evidence for the activity series of metals.
objectives: Observe the deposition of reddish copper
Confirm that zinc is more reactive than copper
Record the progressive decolourisation of the solution

iron-silver-nitrate-displacement.title: Displacement of Silver from Silver Nitrate by Iron
iron-silver-nitrate-displacement.description: Clean iron wire inserted into silver nitrate solution deposits a silvery layer of silver on its surface while the solution gradually turns pale green, indicating that iron is oxidised to iron(II) rather than iron(III) under these conditions.
objectives: Observe the deposition of silver and the development of a pale-green solution
Understand why iron forms iron(II) ions rather than iron(III) ions in this displacement
Practise the surface pre-treatment of metal by removing rust before the experiment

potassium-water-violet-flame.title: Violet Flame from the Reaction of Potassium with Water
potassium-water-violet-flame.description: When a small piece of potassium is dropped into water containing a few drops of phenolphthalein, the metal reacts vigorously and ignites with a violet flame — a more dramatic response than that of sodium, illustrating how the reactivity of Group 1 metals increases down the period.
objectives: Observe the vigorous reaction between potassium and water, including the characteristic violet flame
Compare the relative reactivity of sodium and potassium
Follow safe-handling procedures for alkali metals

silver-chloride-ammonia-dissolve.title: Dissolution of Silver Chloride in Aqueous Ammonia
silver-chloride-ammonia-dissolve.description: A white precipitate of silver chloride dissolves completely when excess aqueous ammonia is added, yielding a clear solution; the coordination equilibrium effectively removes silver ions from the solid phase.
objectives: Observe the dissolution of a white precipitate in aqueous ammonia
Understand how coordination equilibrium shifts the dissolution equilibrium
Identify the conditions under which the silver–ammonia complex ion forms

silver-bromide-ammonia-resist.title: Resistance of Silver Bromide to Aqueous Ammonia
silver-bromide-ammonia-resist.description: Pale-yellow silver bromide remains undissolved even in excess aqueous ammonia, forming a sharp contrast with silver chloride and demonstrating that a smaller solubility product makes it increasingly difficult for ammonia to return ions to solution.
objectives: Compare the behaviour of silver chloride and silver bromide in aqueous ammonia
Understand the competition between the solubility product and the complex-formation stability constant
Recognise the trend of decreasing solubility among the silver halides

silver-iodide-ammonia-resist.title: Extremely Low Solubility of Silver Iodide
silver-iodide-ammonia-resist.description: Yellow silver iodide shows no detectable dissolution in excess aqueous ammonia; it has the smallest solubility product among the common silver halides and is the substance used in cloud seeding.
objectives: Confirm that silver iodide does not dissolve in aqueous ammonia
Arrange the three silver halides in order of decreasing solubility
Appreciate the application of silver iodide in artificial rainfall

silver-bromide-thiosulfate-fixing.title: Dissolution of Silver Bromide in Photographic Fixer
silver-bromide-thiosulfate-fixing.description: Silver bromide, which resists aqueous ammonia, dissolves readily in sodium thiosulfate solution to give a colourless liquid; this reaction is the chemical basis of fixing black-and-white photographs.
objectives: Observe the dissolution of silver bromide in fixer solution
Compare the coordinating ability of ammonia with that of thiosulfate ion
Understand the chemistry underlying photographic fixing

silver-iodide-thiosulfate-limit.title: Silver Iodide Resists Even Photographic Fixer
silver-iodide-thiosulfate-limit.description: Silver iodide remains at the bottom of the test tube when sodium thiosulfate solution is added, showing that even a relatively strong common ligand has its limits; cyanide would be required to bring it into solution.
objectives: Confirm that silver iodide is resistant to dissolution by fixer solution
Appreciate the relative nature of ligand strength
Understand the significance of an extremely small solubility product

silver-carbonate-ammonia-dissolve.title: Dissolution of Silver Carbonate in Aqueous Ammonia
silver-carbonate-ammonia-dissolve.description: Pale-yellow silver carbonate dissolves in aqueous ammonia to give a clear, colourless solution — a route to the silver–ammonia complex that is often overlooked when preparing Tollens' reagent.
objectives: Observe the coordination-driven dissolution of silver carbonate
Compare the ease of dissolution of silver carbonate with that of the silver halides
Become familiar with the various methods of preparing silver–ammonia solution

copper-hydroxide-ammonia-deep-blue.title: Dissolution of Copper(II) Hydroxide in Excess Aqueous Ammonia
copper-hydroxide-ammonia-deep-blue.description: A pale-blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide dissolves in excess aqueous ammonia to give a deep-blue, transparent solution; the pronounced shift in colour from pale blue to deep blue is the most visible indicator of complex-ion formation.
objectives: Observe the dissolution of the precipitate and the accompanying change to a deep-blue colour
Understand the formation of the tetraamminecopper(II) complex ion
Distinguish between the outcomes of adding a limited amount and an excess of aqueous ammonia

zinc-hydroxide-ammonia-dissolve.title: Dissolution of Zinc Hydroxide in Aqueous Ammonia
zinc-hydroxide-ammonia-dissolve.description: White zinc hydroxide dissolves both in strong base and in aqueous ammonia — the former by amphoteric character, the latter by complex formation — yet both pathways lead to the same result.
objectives: Observe the dissolution of the white precipitate in aqueous ammonia
Distinguish between amphoteric dissolution and dissolution by complex formation
Understand the formation of the tetraammineزinc(II) complex ion

nickel-hydroxide-ammonia-violet.title: Dissolution of Nickel(II) Hydroxide in Aqueous Ammonia to Give a Blue-Violet Solution
nickel-hydroxide-ammonia-violet.description: Green nickel(II) hydroxide dissolves in excess aqueous ammonia to yield a blue-violet solution; the colour of the hexaamminenickel(II) complex ion differs markedly from that of the original precipitate.
objectives: Observe the transition from a green precipitate to a blue-violet solution
Recognise the hexacoordinate nickel–ammonia complex ion
Understand the influence of the ligand field on colour

copper-edta-chelate-titration.title: EDTA Chelation Titration of Copper(II) Ions
copper-edta-chelate-titration.description: Addition of EDTA to a pale-blue copper(II) sulfate solution produces a slight deepening of colour; the six donor atoms of EDTA encapsulate the copper(II) ion and release hydrogen ions, so the titration must be carried out in a buffer solution.
objectives: Master the basic procedure of complexometric titration
Understand the 1∶1 stoichiometry of EDTA chelation
Recognise the necessity of a buffer system in complexometric titration

iron3-edta-decolorize.title: Decolourisation of an Iron(III) Salt by EDTA
iron3-edta-decolorize.description: Addition of EDTA to a brown-yellow iron(III) chloride solution produces a pale-yellow colour; once the iron(III) ion is chelated, it no longer exhibits the colour characteristic of its aquo complex.
objectives: Observe the colour change from brown-yellow to pale yellow
Understand how chelation alters the coordination environment of a metal ion
Appreciate the strong chelating ability of EDTA towards high-valence ions

aluminum-edta-back-titration.title: Back-Titration of Aluminium Ions with EDTA
aluminum-edta-back-titration.description: The chelation of aluminium chloride with EDTA is slow and yields a colourless product; EDTA is therefore added in excess and the surplus is back-titrated with a zinc salt — a classic workaround in complexometric analysis.
objectives: Understand the conditions under which back-titration is applicable
Master strategies for handling slow-complexation systems
Recognise why a colourless chelate requires an indicator

lead-edta-masking.title: Masking of Lead(II) Ions with EDTA
lead-edta-masking.description: Addition of EDTA to a lead(II) nitrate solution chelates lead firmly; subsequent addition of sodium sulfide no longer produces a black precipitate, illustrating the standard approach to masking interfering ions.
objectives: Understand the mechanism by which a masking agent operates
Compare precipitation behaviour in the presence and absence of EDTA
Master the use of complexation masking in analytical chemistry

magnesium-edta-hardness.title: Complexation of Magnesium Ions with EDTA
magnesium-edta-hardness.description: Magnesium sulfate reacts with EDTA to form a colourless chelate; Eriochrome Black T is required as an indicator to follow the colour change — providing the second half of the foundation for water-hardness determination.
objectives: Master the complexometric titration of magnesium
Understand why a colourless chelate requires an indicator
Integrate the results for magnesium and calcium to derive the concept of total hardness

zinc-edta-titration.title: Standardisation of EDTA with Zinc Ions
zinc-edta-titration.description: Zinc sulfate reacts quantitatively with EDTA and is commonly used as a primary standard for the standardisation of EDTA solutions; the end point is determined by the sharp colour change of the indicator.
objectives: Master the operational procedure for standardising EDTA
Understand the criteria for selecting a primary standard
Record the colour change at the end point

nickel-edta-blue-green.title: EDTA Chelation of Nickel(II)
nickel-edta-blue-green.description: Addition of EDTA to a green nickel(II) chloride solution produces a blue-green complex, as the chelating ligand displaces coordinated water molecules and alters the ligand field around the metal center.
objectives: Observe the subtle color shift from green to blue-green
Understand how ligand substitution influences the color of a coordination compound
Learn the conditions required for complexometric titration of nickel(II) with EDTA

cobalt-edta-purple-red.title: EDTA Chelation of Cobalt(II)
cobalt-edta-purple-red.description: Addition of EDTA to a pink cobalt(II) chloride solution yields a purple-red complex, a color change that is opposite in direction to the blue color produced by chloro-coordination, making the two systems a useful visual contrast.
objectives: Observe the color transition from pink to purple-red
Compare the opposing effects of EDTA and chloride ligands on the color of cobalt(II) complexes
Understand how ligand-field strength determines the direction of a color change

copper-chloride-ammonia-blue.title: Deep-Blue Ammine Complex of Copper(II) Chloride
copper-chloride-ammonia-blue.description: Excess aqueous ammonia added to a blue-green copper(II) chloride solution produces a deep-blue tetraamminecopper(II) complex, illustrating how the same metal ion displays distinctly different colors under chloro and ammine coordination.
objectives: Observe the color change from blue-green to deep blue
Compare the colors of the chloro and ammine complexes of copper(II)
Identify the criteria for judging whether ligand exchange has occurred

copper-nitrate-ammonia-blue.title: Ammine Coordination of Copper(II) Nitrate
copper-nitrate-ammonia-blue.description: Addition of excess aqueous ammonia to copper(II) nitrate solution also yields a deep-blue complex, demonstrating that coordination behavior is determined by the interaction between the central cation and its ligands, while the counter-anion plays no significant role.
objectives: Confirm that the counter-anion does not affect the color of a coordination compound
Reinforce the conditions for formation of the tetraamminecopper(II) ion
Understand the concept of the central ion in coordination chemistry

iron3-sulfate-thiocyanate-red.title: Blood-Red Thiocyanate Test for Iron(III) Sulfate
iron3-sulfate-thiocyanate-red.description: Addition of potassium thiocyanate to an iron(III) sulfate solution instantly produces a blood-red color; this is the most sensitive test for Fe³⁺, and the reaction is visible even at trace concentrations.
objectives: Master the thiocyanate test for iron(III) ions
Appreciate the sensitivity of a colorimetric test reaction
Confirm that the anion present does not interfere with the color response

benzene-bromination-substitution.title: Electrophilic Bromination of Benzene
benzene-bromination-substitution.description: Benzene reacts with liquid bromine in the presence of iron powder as a catalyst via electrophilic substitution; the hydrogen bromide evolved turns moist litmus red, and the product bromobenzene separates as a water-insoluble oil.
objectives: Distinguish between substitution and addition reactions
Learn how to test for hydrogen bromide gas
Observe the separation of the oily product into a distinct layer

toluene-bromination-substitution.title: Ring Bromination of Toluene
toluene-bromination-substitution.description: Toluene undergoes ring bromination in the presence of iron powder to give bromotoluene and hydrogen bromide; the reaction proceeds more readily than that of benzene, showing that the methyl group activates the aromatic ring.
objectives: Compare the relative reactivity of benzene and toluene toward electrophilic substitution
Understand how an alkyl substituent activates the benzene ring
Test for the hydrogen bromide released during the reaction

toluene-side-chain-oxidation.title: Oxidation of the Toluene Side Chain to Benzoic Acid
toluene-side-chain-oxidation.description: Heating toluene with acidic potassium permanganate solution decolorizes the purple reagent as the methyl group is oxidized to a carboxyl group; white crystals of benzoic acid precipitate upon cooling.
objectives: Recognize that the benzene ring activates its side chain toward oxidation
Confirm that the benzene ring itself is not oxidized under these conditions
Practice filtration and recrystallization to isolate the product

acetylene-bromine-addition.title: Addition of Acetylene to Bromine Water
acetylene-bromine-addition.description: When acetylene is bubbled into bromine water, the orange-yellow colour disappears rapidly without any gas being evolved. The triple bond undergoes two successive addition steps, consuming twice as much bromine as ethylene does.
objectives: Observe the decolorisation of bromine water with no gas evolution
Compare the addition reactivity of a triple bond with that of a double bond
Distinguish between addition reactions and substitution reactions

acetylene-kmno4-oxidation.title: Decolorisation of Acidic Potassium Permanganate by Acetylene
acetylene-kmno4-oxidation.description: When acetylene is bubbled into acidic potassium permanganate solution, the purple-red colour fades and carbon dioxide is evolved, indicating that the triple bond is completely oxidised and cleaved.
objectives: Observe simultaneous decolorisation and gas evolution
Recognise oxidative cleavage of unsaturated bonds
Apply the test as a qualitative method for identifying unsaturated hydrocarbons

styrene-bromine-addition.title: Addition across the Side-Chain Double Bond of Styrene
styrene-bromine-addition.description: When styrene is added dropwise to bromine water, decolorisation occurs at the side-chain double bond rather than at the benzene ring, and no catalyst is required.
objectives: Confirm that addition takes place at the side chain rather than at the benzene ring
Compare the behaviour of benzene and styrene towards bromine water
Understand the reactivity of a double bond within a conjugated system

ethylene-glycol-sodium-hydrogen.title: Determination of Hydroxyl Group Count in Ethylene Glycol by Reaction with Sodium
ethylene-glycol-sodium-hydrogen.description: The volume of hydrogen gas evolved when ethylene glycol reacts with sodium is twice that produced by an equimolar monohydric alcohol. The amount of gas evolved can therefore be used to deduce the number of hydroxyl groups in the molecule.
objectives: Determine the number of hydroxyl groups from the volume of hydrogen gas evolved
Compare hydrogen gas yields from monohydric and dihydric alcohols
Develop the technique of quantitative gas collection

glycerol-sodium-three-hydroxyl.title: Hydrogen Evolution from the Three Hydroxyl Groups of Glycerol Reacting with Sodium
glycerol-sodium-three-hydroxyl.description: Glycerol contains three hydroxyl groups; accordingly, the volume of hydrogen gas evolved on reaction with sodium is three times that from a monohydric alcohol. Bubbles form steadily along the surface of the sodium but the reaction is not vigorous.
objectives: Verify the stoichiometry of hydrogen evolution from a trihydric alcohol
Compare the reactivity of hydroxyl groups in alcohols with that in water
Understand the structural features of polyhydric alcohols

propanol-sodium-hydrogen.title: Displacement of Hydrogen Gas from Propanol by Sodium
propanol-sodium-hydrogen.description: Propanol reacts with sodium to evolve hydrogen gas slowly. The longer carbon chain slightly reduces the reactivity of the hydroxyl group, and bubbles form more slowly than in systems with short-chain alcohols.
objectives: Observe that the rate of hydrogen evolution decreases as the carbon chain lengthens
Understand the influence of the alkyl group on hydroxyl group reactivity
Identify the conditions required for the formation of sodium alkoxides

aniline-bromine-white-precipitate.title: Trisubstitution of Aniline with Bromine Water
aniline-bromine-white-precipitate.description: When aniline is added dropwise to bromine water, the colour disappears immediately and a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline forms without the need for a catalyst. This demonstrates that the amino group activates the benzene ring more strongly than a hydroxyl group does.
objectives: Observe the formation of a white precipitate via trisubstitution at room temperature
Compare the activating effects of the amino group and the hydroxyl group
Contrast this reaction with the iron-powder-catalysed monosubstitution of benzene

benzaldehyde-silver-mirror.title: Silver Mirror Reaction of Benzaldehyde
benzaldehyde-silver-mirror.description: When benzaldehyde is heated in a water bath with silver–ammonia solution, a bright silver coating forms on the inner wall of the test tube, confirming that the aldehyde group of an aromatic aldehyde is also reducing. The silver–ammonia solution is prepared from silver nitrate and aqueous ammonia.
objectives: Master the procedural requirements of the silver mirror reaction
Confirm the reducing property of an aromatic aldehyde
Understand the effect of tube-wall cleanliness on the quality of the silver mirror

benzoic-acid-ethyl-ester.title: Synthesis of Ethyl Benzoate
benzoic-acid-ethyl-ester.description: Benzoic acid undergoes esterification with ethanol in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid as a catalyst, producing ethyl benzoate, a fruity-smelling ester that is insoluble in water and floats on the surface.
objectives: Master the esterification conditions for aromatic acids
Understand the function of a reflux assembly
Learn to separate the ester layer using a separating funnel

propanoic-acid-ethyl-ester.title: Synthesis of Ethyl Propanoate
propanoic-acid-ethyl-ester.description: Propionic acid undergoes esterification with ethanol to yield ethyl propanoate, whose fruity odor is more pronounced than that of shorter-chain esters, making it a clear illustration of how chain length affects scent.
objectives: Compare the odors of esters derived from different carboxylic acids
Master the general conditions for esterification
Understand strategies for improving the yield of a reversible reaction

acetic-acid-propyl-ester.title: Synthesis of Propyl Acetate
acetic-acid-propyl-ester.description: Acetic acid undergoes esterification with propanol to produce propyl acetate, which has a characteristic pear-like fragrance, demonstrating that a series of fragrances can be obtained from a single carboxylic acid by varying the alcohol.
objectives: Understand the effect of the alcohol carbon chain on the odor of the resulting ester
Consolidate esterification technique
Recognize the application of esters in the fragrance industry

acetic-acid-butyl-ester.title: Synthesis of n-Butyl Acetate
acetic-acid-butyl-ester.description: Acetic acid undergoes esterification with n-butanol to produce n-butyl acetate, a widely used coating solvent whose relatively high boiling point requires a prolonged reflux period.
objectives: Master the reflux synthesis of a high-boiling-point ester
Understand the relationship between boiling point and carbon chain length
Recognize the preparation route for industrial solvents

sucrose-acid-hydrolysis.title: Acid Hydrolysis of Sucrose
sucrose-acid-hydrolysis.description: Sucrose is hydrolyzed to monosaccharides by heating in a water bath in the presence of dilute sulfuric acid as a catalyst; the solution, initially non-reducing, acquires reducing properties that can be detected by the silver mirror reaction.
objectives: Recognize the hydrolysis of a disaccharide
Understand the role of acid catalysis in hydrolysis
Master the pre-treatment of hydrolysis products before testing

cellulose-acid-hydrolysis.title: Acid Hydrolysis of Cellulose
cellulose-acid-hydrolysis.description: Absorbent cotton is gradually hydrolyzed to glucose by prolonged heating in concentrated sulfuric acid, a process considerably more difficult than the hydrolysis of most polysaccharides and one that represents the fundamental route for producing sugars from biomass.
objectives: Compare the relative difficulty of hydrolyzing cellulose versus starch
Understand how the crystalline regions of cellulose impede hydrolysis
Recognize the industrial significance of biomass-to-sugar conversion

copper-sulfate-dissolution-exotherm.title: Exothermic Dissolution of Anhydrous Copper(II) Sulfate
copper-sulfate-dissolution-exotherm.description: When white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate dissolves in water, the enthalpy of hydration is substantial; the thermometer reading rises noticeably and the solution turns blue, a process that also serves as the basis for detecting trace amounts of water.
objectives: Measure the temperature change during the dissolution process
Understand the competition between hydration enthalpy and lattice energy
Recognize the principle underlying the use of anhydrous copper(II) sulfate as a test for water

sodium-acetate-dissolution-endotherm.title: Endothermic Dissolution of Sodium Acetate
sodium-acetate-dissolution-endotherm.description: When sodium acetate dissolves in water, the energy required to break down the crystal lattice exceeds the hydration enthalpy, causing the thermometer reading to fall — in direct contrast to the exothermic crystallization observed with its supersaturated solution.
objectives: Record the temperature decrease associated with endothermic dissolution
Compare crystallization exotherm with dissolution endotherm to understand process reversibility
Master the sign convention for enthalpy of solution

ammonium-sulfate-dissolution-endotherm.title: Dissolution of Ammonium Sulfate — Endothermic Process
ammonium-sulfate-dissolution-endotherm.description: When ammonium sulfate dissolves in water, the temperature drops noticeably. Like ammonium nitrate, it is an endothermic solute and is one reason why soil surface temperature decreases briefly after nitrogen fertiliser application.
objectives: Measure the heat absorbed during dissolution of an ammonium salt
Compare the temperature drop produced by different ammonium salts
Connect experimental observations to the practical context of agricultural fertilisation

potassium-chloride-dissolution-endotherm.title: Dissolution of Potassium Chloride — Endothermic Process
potassium-chloride-dissolution-endotherm.description: When potassium chloride dissolves in water, the temperature falls slightly. The endothermic effect is far smaller than that of ammonium nitrate, making this system suitable for comparing the enthalpy of dissolution of different salts.
objectives: Measure the small temperature change associated with a weakly endothermic dissolution
Compare the magnitude of dissolution enthalpies for different salts
Practise accurate quantitative sample weighing

aluminum-chloride-dissolution-exotherm.title: Dissolution of Aluminium Chloride — Vigorous Exothermic Process
aluminum-chloride-dissolution-exotherm.description: When anhydrous aluminium chloride dissolves in water, hydration and hydrolysis both release heat simultaneously, causing a pronounced temperature rise accompanied by a pungent odour; the solid must therefore be added slowly.
objectives: Observe the vigorous exothermic effect during dissolution of a high-oxidation-state salt
Understand the contribution of hydrolysis to the overall thermal effect
Learn safe addition technique for readily hydrolysed salts

sodium-nitrate-dissolution-endotherm.title: Dissolution of Sodium Nitrate — Endothermic Process
sodium-nitrate-dissolution-endotherm.description: When sodium nitrate dissolves in water, the temperature falls. This endothermic trend is consistent with that of potassium nitrate, another nitrate salt, indicating that nitrate salts generally have lattice energies that outweigh their hydration enthalpies.
objectives: Measure the heat absorbed during dissolution of a nitrate salt
Generalise the influence of the anion on dissolution enthalpy
Practise correct thermometer reading technique

sodium-sulfate-dissolution-endotherm.title: Dissolution of Sodium Sulfate — Endothermic Process
sodium-sulfate-dissolution-endotherm.description: Anhydrous sodium sulfate dissolves in water with a slight temperature decrease, whereas its decahydrate shows a more pronounced endothermic effect; the comparison illustrates the contribution of water of crystallisation to the enthalpy of dissolution.
objectives: Measure the endothermic dissolution of sodium sulfate
Understand the effect of water of crystallisation on the thermal outcome
Design a controlled comparison experiment using equal amounts of substance

potassium-bromide-dissolution-endotherm.title: Dissolution of Potassium Bromide — Endothermic Process
potassium-bromide-dissolution-endotherm.description: When potassium bromide dissolves in water, the temperature drops slightly. Together with potassium chloride and potassium iodide, it forms a series that illustrates the trend in dissolution enthalpy across the Group 17 halides.
objectives: Measure the heat absorbed during dissolution of potassium bromide
Arrange the Group 17 potassium halides in order of endothermic effect
Appreciate how ionic radius influences lattice energy

potassium-iodide-dissolution-endotherm.title: Dissolution of Potassium Iodide — Endothermic Process
potassium-iodide-dissolution-endotherm.description: When potassium iodide dissolves in water, the temperature falls. Although the iodide ion has the largest radius and the lowest lattice energy in the halide series, dissolution remains endothermic, indicating that the hydration enthalpy decreases proportionally.
objectives: Measure the heat absorbed during dissolution of potassium iodide
Analyse the parallel changes in lattice energy and hydration enthalpy
Compile and organise the data set for the complete potassium halide series

magnesium-chloride-dissolution-exotherm.title: Dissolution of Magnesium Chloride — Exothermic Process
magnesium-chloride-dissolution-exotherm.description: Anhydrous magnesium chloride releases considerable heat on dissolving in water. The high charge density of the magnesium ion results in a large hydration enthalpy, which explains why temperature control is necessary during salt production from brine.
objectives: Measure the heat released during dissolution of a divalent salt
Understand the relationship between ionic charge density and hydration enthalpy
Connect the experimental findings to temperature-control requirements in the brine industry

calcium-chloride-dissolution-exotherm.title: Dissolution of Calcium Chloride: Exothermic Process and Heat Packs
calcium-chloride-dissolution-exotherm.description: Dissolving anhydrous calcium chloride in water causes a rapid rise in temperature, making it a common heat-generating agent in chemical heat packs — a useful contrast to ammonium nitrate cold packs.
objectives: Measure the temperature increase produced by dissolving calcium chloride
Understand the chemical principle underlying heat packs
Learn the basic procedure for thermally insulated calorimetry

magnesium-sulfate-dissolution-exotherm.title: Exothermic Dissolution of Magnesium Sulfate
magnesium-sulfate-dissolution-exotherm.description: Anhydrous magnesium sulfate releases heat when dissolved in water, whereas the heptahydrate (Epsom salt) absorbs heat on dissolution — a classic example of how water of crystallization can reverse the sign of the enthalpy change.
objectives: Measure the heat released when anhydrous magnesium sulfate dissolves
Compare the endothermic dissolution of the hydrated form
Understand how water of crystallization can change the sign of the thermal effect

sodium-carbonate-dissolution-exotherm.title: Exothermic Dissolution of Sodium Carbonate
sodium-carbonate-dissolution-exotherm.description: Soda ash releases heat when dissolved in water and, owing to hydrolysis, produces an alkaline solution; any undissolved solid remains visible, providing two simultaneous observations: a thermal effect and a change in pH.
objectives: Measure the heat released during dissolution of sodium carbonate
Monitor the alkalinity of the resulting solution simultaneously
Distinguish between the contributions of the heat of dissolution and the heat of hydrolysis

ammonium-chloride-dissolution-endotherm.title: Endothermic Dissolution of Ammonium Chloride
ammonium-chloride-dissolution-endotherm.description: Dissolving ammonium chloride in water causes the temperature to fall; ammonium salts produce a large cooling effect and are inexpensive, making them a common substitute in improvised instant cold packs.
objectives: Measure the heat absorbed when ammonium chloride dissolves
Compare the cooling efficiency of different ammonium salts
Design a simple instant-cold-pack formulation

barium-hydroxide-dissolution-endotherm.title: Endothermic Dissolution of Barium Hydroxide
barium-hydroxide-dissolution-endotherm.description: Barium hydroxide absorbs heat when dissolved in water, making it one of the few strong bases whose dissolution is endothermic — a striking contrast to the exothermic dissolution exhibited by most strong bases.
objectives: Measure the atypical heat absorption during dissolution of a strong base
Compare this endothermic behaviour with the exothermic dissolution of sodium hydroxide
Follow proper safety procedures when handling strong bases

thiosulfate-dissolution-endotherm.title: Endothermic Dissolution of Sodium Thiosulfate
thiosulfate-dissolution-endotherm.description: Sodium thiosulfate absorbs heat when dissolved in water, yet its supersaturated solution releases heat upon crystallization — making it a classic model for phase-change thermal-storage materials.
objectives: Measure the heat absorbed when sodium thiosulfate dissolves
Understand the reversible energy storage associated with phase change
Learn how to prepare a supersaturated solution

sodium-bicarbonate-dissolution-endotherm.title: Endothermic Dissolution of Sodium Bicarbonate
sodium-bicarbonate-dissolution-endotherm.description: Sodium bicarbonate has limited solubility and absorbs heat on dissolution, leaving undissolved solid visible; the experiment allows simultaneous observation of an endothermic effect and the solubility limit.
objectives: Measure the heat absorbed when sodium bicarbonate dissolves
Observe the solubility limit and the presence of residual undissolved solid
Distinguish between solubility and rate of dissolution

zinc-copper-sulfate-calorimetry.title: Calorimetric Determination of the Reaction Enthalpy for the Displacement of Copper by Zinc
zinc-copper-sulfate-calorimetry.description: When zinc powder is added to a copper(II) sulfate solution, the blue colour fades, red copper deposits, and the temperature rises noticeably; the enthalpy change of the displacement reaction can be estimated from the observed temperature increase.
objectives: Estimate the enthalpy change of the displacement reaction from the measured temperature rise
Observe the colour change and heat release simultaneously
Learn to use a simple calorimeter

magnesium-hydrochloric-calorimetry.title: Calorimetric Determination of the Enthalpy of Reaction between Magnesium and Hydrochloric Acid
magnesium-hydrochloric-calorimetry.description: When magnesium ribbon is added to hydrochloric acid, hydrogen gas evolves vigorously and the temperature rises rapidly. The temperature change recorded with an insulated cup can be used to calculate the molar enthalpy of reaction.
objectives: Determine the heat released by the reaction between a metal and an acid
Calculate the molar enthalpy of reaction from calorimetric data
Analyse the systematic error introduced by heat loss to the surroundings

sodium-peroxide-water-exotherm.title: Exothermic Reaction and Oxygen Evolution from Sodium Peroxide and Water
sodium-peroxide-water-exotherm.description: When sodium peroxide is added to water, gas bubbles are released and the temperature rises markedly; the heat evolved is sufficient to ignite a glowing splint, demonstrating that sodium peroxide acts simultaneously as an oxygen-releasing agent and a heat source.
objectives: Observe oxygen evolution and heat release occurring simultaneously
Verify that the heat produced can ignite a glowing wooden splint
Handle peroxide compounds safely according to established procedures

thermite-iron-oxide-enthalpy.title: Heat Release and Enthalpy Estimation for the Thermite Reaction
thermite-iron-oxide-enthalpy.description: When a mixture of aluminium powder and iron(III) oxide is ignited, intense sparks are produced, molten iron forms, and a large quantity of heat is released; the temperature of the products can be used to make a rough estimate of the reaction enthalpy.
objectives: Infer the magnitude of heat release from the observation of molten product formation
Estimate the order of magnitude of the enthalpy change from the state of the products
Apply appropriate safety precautions when working with high-temperature reactions

nickel-hydroxide-green-identification.title: Identification of Nickel(II) Ions by the Apple-Green Precipitate
nickel-hydroxide-green-identification.description: Addition of sodium hydroxide to a nickel(II) sulfate solution produces a distinctive apple-green precipitate of nickel(II) hydroxide, whose colour provides a direct visual criterion for identifying nickel(II) ions.
objectives: Identify nickel(II) ions by the characteristic colour of their hydroxide precipitate
Distinguish between transition metal ions of the same group by precipitate colour
Carry out dropwise addition and observation according to standard laboratory technique

cobalt-hydroxide-pink-identification.title: Identification of Cobalt(II) Ions by the Pink Precipitate
cobalt-hydroxide-pink-identification.description: Addition of alkali to a cobalt(II) chloride solution yields a pink precipitate of cobalt(II) hydroxide, which turns brown on prolonged exposure to air through oxidation; this behaviour may be compared directly with the apple-green precipitate formed by nickel(II) ions.
objectives: Identify cobalt(II) ions by the characteristic colour of their hydroxide precipitate
Observe the colour change that accompanies aerial oxidation of the precipitate
Distinguish between cobalt(II) and nickel(II) ions by comparative observation

manganese-hydroxide-brown-identification.title: Identification of Manganese(II) Ions by the White-to-Brown Precipitate Transition
manganese-hydroxide-brown-identification.description: Addition of alkali to a manganese(II) sulfate solution initially produces a white precipitate of manganese(II) hydroxide, which rapidly turns brown upon exposure to air; this colour transition serves as the diagnostic criterion for manganese(II) ions.
objectives: Identify manganese(II) ions by the characteristic colour change of their hydroxide precipitate
Record the time course of the white-to-brown transition
Understand the tendency of lower-oxidation-state manganese compounds to undergo oxidation

silver-chromate-mohr-endpoint.title: Potassium Chromate as End-Point Indicator in the Mohr Method
silver-chromate-mohr-endpoint.description: In the titration of chloride ions using potassium chromate as indicator, once the chloride ions have been consumed, silver ions react with chromate ions to form a brick-red precipitate of silver chromate, signalling the end point.
objectives: Understand the principle by which the end point is indicated in a precipitation titration
Observe the appearance of the brick-red end point
Apply the correct operating conditions required by the Mohr method

lead-chromate-yellow-identification.title: Identification of Lead(II) Ions by the Chrome Yellow Precipitate
lead-chromate-yellow-identification.description: Addition of potassium chromate to a lead(II) nitrate solution produces a bright yellow precipitate of lead(II) chromate — the pigment known historically as chrome yellow — which serves as the classical qualitative criterion for the presence of lead(II) ions.
objectives: Identify lead(II) ions by precipitation with chromate
Recognise the chemical composition of the pigment chrome yellow
Understand the requirements for the safe disposal of heavy-metal waste solutions

barium-chromate-pale-yellow.title: Identification of Barium Ion by Pale-Yellow Chromate Precipitate
barium-chromate-pale-yellow.description: Adding potassium chromate to a barium chloride solution produces a pale-yellow barium chromate precipitate, which can be distinguished from the pure-white barium sulfate precipitate by colour alone.
objectives: Master the identification of barium ion using chromate
Compare the colour difference between the two barium precipitates
Understand the value of precipitate colour in qualitative analysis

strontium-sulfate-white-identification.title: Identification of Strontium Ion by Sulfate Precipitation
strontium-sulfate-white-identification.description: Adding sodium sulfate to a strontium chloride solution produces a white strontium sulfate precipitate; its solubility lies between those of calcium sulfate and barium sulfate, which makes fractional precipitation feasible.
objectives: Master the identification of strontium ion using sulfate
Arrange the solubilities of alkaline-earth metal sulfates in order
Understand the rationale for separation by fractional precipitation

strontium-carbonate-acid-soluble.title: Formation of Strontium Carbonate Precipitate and Verification by Acid Dissolution
