strontium-carbonate-acid-soluble.description: Mixing strontium nitrate with sodium carbonate produces a white strontium carbonate precipitate; adding dilute acid then dissolves the precipitate with effervescence, and the two observations together confirm the carbonate identity.
objectives: Form and confirm the strontium carbonate precipitate
Use acid dissolution to verify the composition of the precipitate
Master the analytical logic of two-step verification

zinc-hydroxide-white-identification.title: White Precipitate of Zinc Ion and Verification of Amphoteric Behaviour
zinc-hydroxide-white-identification.description: Adding a measured amount of sodium hydroxide to zinc sulfate produces a white zinc hydroxide precipitate; continued addition of alkali redissolves the precipitate, and this amphoteric behaviour serves as the diagnostic criterion for the zinc ion.
objectives: Master the precipitate-based identification of zinc ion
Verify the amphoteric dissolution of zinc hydroxide
Appreciate the importance of controlling reagent quantities

silver-phosphate-yellow-identification.title: Identification of Phosphate Ion by Yellow Silver Salt
silver-phosphate-yellow-identification.description: Adding silver nitrate to a sodium phosphate solution produces a yellow silver phosphate precipitate that is soluble in dilute nitric acid, allowing it to be distinguished from the white silver chloride precipitate.
objectives: Master the qualitative identification of phosphate ion
Use acid solubility to differentiate silver salt precipitates
Follow proper procedures for recovering silver salt waste

lead-sulfide-black-identification.title: Identification of Sulfide Ion by Black Lead Salt
lead-sulfide-black-identification.description: Adding lead(II) nitrate to a sodium sulfide solution immediately produces a black lead sulfide precipitate of such intense colour that even trace amounts of sulfide ion are detectable.
objectives: Master the high-sensitivity identification of sulfide ion
Understand the detection principle of lead sulfide test paper
Follow safe procedures for handling sulfur-containing waste

lead-iodide-yellow-identification.title: Identification of Lead Ion by Yellow Iodide Precipitate
lead-iodide-yellow-identification.description: In a dilute nitric acid medium, adding potassium iodide to the test solution produces a bright-yellow lead iodide precipitate, confirming the presence of lead ion; this result can be cross-checked against the chromate method.
objectives: Master the iodide-based identification of lead ion
Cross-validate conclusions with the chromate method
Understand the effect of medium acidity on identification

lithium-chloride-flame-crimson.title: Identification of Lithium Salt by Crimson Flame Colour
lithium-chloride-flame-crimson.description: Lithium chloride releases a slight amount of heat on dissolving; a wire dipped in the solution and held in a flame produces a crimson colour, which can be distinguished from the yellow of sodium and the violet of potassium in a side-by-side comparison.
objectives: Master the characteristic flame colour of lithium
Complete a comparative flame test across the alkali metals
Follow correct procedures for heating and cleaning the platinum wire

dichromate-ferrous-titration.title: Color endpoint of potassium dichromate titration of iron(II)
dichromate-ferrous-titration.description: When potassium dichromate is added dropwise to an iron(II) sulfate solution, the orange-yellow hexavalent chromium is reduced to green trivalent chromium with the release of heat; the sharp color change marks the titration endpoint.
objectives: Master the potassium dichromate method for determining iron(II)
Identify the endpoint by the transition from orange-yellow to green
Compare the advantages and disadvantages of this method with the potassium permanganate method

permanganate-ferrous-titration.title: Self-indication in potassium permanganate titration of iron(II)
permanganate-ferrous-titration.description: Under acidic conditions, potassium permanganate is added dropwise to iron(II) sulfate; the purple-red color fades immediately with each addition, and the endpoint is reached when the last drop no longer fades, requiring no external indicator.
objectives: Master the self-indication principle of the potassium permanganate method
Accurately identify the endpoint at which the purple-red color persists
Analyze the effect of acidity on the titration

oxalate-permanganate-standardization.title: Standardization of potassium permanganate solution with oxalic acid
oxalate-permanganate-standardization.description: Primary-standard oxalic acid is used to titrate potassium permanganate in a hot acidic solution; the purple-red color fades with the release of heat, and the accurate concentration of potassium permanganate is back-calculated from the volume consumed.
objectives: Standardize an oxidizing agent solution using a primary standard
Master temperature control in hot titrations
Calculate the standardization result and relative deviation

iodine-thiosulfate-standardize.title: Standardization of iodine solution with sodium thiosulfate
iodine-thiosulfate-standardize.description: Sodium thiosulfate is added dropwise to a brown-yellow iodine solution; the color gradually fades to colorless, giving a sharp endpoint. This is the fundamental standardization procedure in iodometric analysis.
objectives: Master the standardization procedure for iodometric analysis
Identify the endpoint by the transition from brown-yellow to colorless
Understand the correct timing for adding the starch indicator

ammonium-alkali-gas-endotherm.title: Endothermic evolution of ammonia gas from ammonium salt and alkali
ammonium-alkali-gas-endotherm.description: Mixing ammonium chloride with sodium hydroxide produces pungent ammonia gas and causes the temperature to drop; the gas turns moist red litmus blue, and this dual observation confirms the presence of ammonium ions.
objectives: Confirm the presence of ammonium ions using the dual evidence of gas evolution and color change to blue
Record the endothermic temperature decrease of the reaction
Follow proper technique for smelling gases safely

sulfite-acid-gas-identification.title: Identification of sulfite by gas evolution and decolorization
sulfite-acid-gas-identification.description: Adding hydrochloric acid to sodium sulfite evolves pungent sulfur dioxide with the release of heat; passing the gas into fuchsin solution causes decolorization, providing a confirmatory combination test for sulfite ions.
objectives: Master the gas-evolution test for identifying sulfite ions
Confirm sulfur dioxide by decolorization of fuchsin solution
Implement appropriate protective measures when handling pungent gases

iron3-thiocyanate-colorimetry.title: Colorimetric determination of iron content with thiocyanate
iron3-thiocyanate-colorimetry.description: Iron(III) chloride reacts with potassium thiocyanate to form a blood-red complex whose color intensity increases with iron concentration; comparison against a standard color series allows semi-quantitative determination of iron.
objectives: Prepare a standard color comparison series
Perform semi-quantitative iron determination by visual colorimetry
Analyze the sources of error in colorimetric analysis

tin-silver-nitrate-galvanic.title: Verification of the potential difference between tin and silver by displacement
tin-silver-nitrate-galvanic.description: When tin foil / tin sheet is immersed in a silver nitrate solution, silvery crystalline dendrites deposit on the surface with the release of heat, demonstrating that the standard electrode potential of tin is lower than that of silver and that tin undergoes spontaneous oxidation.
objectives: Determine the relative order of electrode potentials from the direction of displacement
Observe the deposition of silver dendrites and the associated heat release
Master the surface preparation of metal electrodes by polishing

nickel-copper-sulfate-galvanic.title: Verification of the Nickel–Copper Potential Difference by Displacement
nickel-copper-sulfate-galvanic.description: When a nickel strip is placed in a copper(II) sulfate solution, a red copper layer deposits on its surface and heat is released while the blue colour fades, providing direct evidence that nickel precedes copper in the electrochemical series.
objectives: Determine the relative positions of nickel and copper in the electrochemical series
Observe the formation of a displacement coating
Understand the relationship between spontaneous reactions and cell electromotive force

tin-copper-sulfate-galvanic.title: Verification of the Tin–Copper Potential Difference by Displacement
tin-copper-sulfate-galvanic.description: When a tin foil / tin sheet is immersed in a copper(II) sulfate solution, red copper deposits slowly and a slight temperature rise is observed; the reaction proceeds more slowly than with zinc, reflecting the weaker driving force associated with a smaller potential difference.
objectives: Compare reaction rates at different potential differences
Understand the effect of electromotive force on driving force
Record the time data of the displacement process

cadmium-copper-sulfate-galvanic.title: Verification of the Cadmium–Copper Potential Difference by Displacement
cadmium-copper-sulfate-galvanic.description: When a cadmium sheet is placed in a copper(II) sulfate solution, red copper is displaced and heat is released; because cadmium is the negative-electrode material in nickel–cadmium batteries, this experiment illustrates its tendency to lose electrons.
objectives: Verify the position of cadmium in the activity series
Connect the findings to the choice of negative-electrode material in nickel–cadmium batteries
Establish proper procedures for the protection and recovery of heavy-metal waste

nickel-silver-nitrate-galvanic.title: Verification of the Nickel–Silver Potential Difference by Displacement
nickel-silver-nitrate-galvanic.description: When a nickel strip is immersed in a silver nitrate solution, a grey silver coating deposits on its surface and heat is released; comparison with the tin–silver pair allows the relative order of nickel, tin, and silver in the electrochemical series to be established.
objectives: Establish the electrochemical series order of the three metals
Observe the formation process of the silver coating
Learn the recovery procedure for waste solutions containing precious metals

lead-copper-sulfate-galvanic.title: Verification of the Lead–Copper Potential Difference by Displacement
lead-copper-sulfate-galvanic.description: When a lead strip is immersed in a copper(II) sulfate solution, red copper deposits on its surface and heat is released; because lead is the negative-electrode material in lead–acid batteries, this experiment corroborates its tendency to lose electrons.
objectives: Verify that lead precedes copper in the electrochemical series
Connect the findings to the choice of negative electrode in lead–acid batteries
Follow correct procedures for the disposal of lead-containing waste solutions

lead-silver-nitrate-galvanic.title: Verification of the Lead–Silver Potential Difference by Displacement
lead-silver-nitrate-galvanic.description: When a lead strip is placed in a silver nitrate solution, silver dendrites grow on its surface and heat is released; the well-defined dendritic morphology provides a macroscopic demonstration of electrocrystallisation growth.
objectives: Observe the morphology of dendrites formed by displacement
Understand the nucleation and growth processes of electrocrystallisation
Follow correct procedures for handling silver salt solutions

magnesium-silver-nitrate-galvanic.title: Vigorous Displacement Driven by the Large Magnesium–Silver Potential Difference
magnesium-silver-nitrate-galvanic.description: When magnesium ribbon is inserted into a silver nitrate solution, a large amount of silver deposits rapidly and a pronounced temperature rise is observed; the reaction is the most vigorous because the potential difference is the largest, and it may be compared directly with the lead–silver pair.
objectives: Compare the vigour of reactions at large and small potential differences
Record the temperature rise quantitatively
Build an intuitive connection between electromotive force and reaction rate

magnesium-copper-sulfate-galvanic.title: Displacement Verification of the Spontaneous Reaction Underlying the Magnesium–Copper Galvanic Cell
magnesium-copper-sulfate-galvanic.description: When magnesium ribbon is placed in a copper(II) sulfate solution, red copper is displaced rapidly and a significant temperature rise is observed while the blue colour fades quickly, demonstrating the spontaneous reaction that underlies the magnesium–copper galvanic cell.
objectives: Confirm the spontaneous reaction of the magnesium–copper galvanic cell
Observe the fading of the blue colour of the solution
Understand the distinct roles of the two electrodes in a galvanic cell

aluminum-copper-sulfate-galvanic.title: Aluminium Strip in Copper(II) Sulfate: Passive Film and Displacement
aluminum-copper-sulfate-galvanic.description: When an aluminium strip is immersed in a copper(II) sulfate solution, the native oxide film must first be removed before copper deposits and heat is released, demonstrating that the passive film blocks the electrode reaction.
objectives: Understand how a passive film inhibits electrode reactions
Learn the pre-treatment method for removing the oxide film
Observe the onset of displacement after the film has been removed

ferric-chloride-copper-etching.title: Etching Copper Foil with Iron(III) Chloride to Fabricate a Circuit Board
ferric-chloride-copper-etching.description: A copper strip immersed in an iron(III) chloride solution dissolves gradually; the brown-yellow solution turns blue-green and releases heat, illustrating the chemical etching principle used in printed-circuit-board manufacture.
objectives: Understand the electron transfer involved when iron(III) chloride etches copper
Determine the concentration and temperature conditions required for the etchant
Follow correct procedures for recovering and disposing of copper-containing waste solution

ferric-sulfate-copper-etching.title: Controlled Experiment: Etching Copper with Iron(III) Sulfate
ferric-sulfate-copper-etching.description: An iron(III) sulfate solution dissolves copper with heat evolution in the same manner as iron(III) chloride, showing that etching depends on the oxidising power of Fe³⁺ rather than on the identity of the anion.
objectives: Verify the influence of the anion on the rate of etching
Compare the etching rates of the two etchant solutions
Generalise that oxidising power, not anion type, determines whether a reaction proceeds

iron-ferric-comproportionation-cell.title: Comproportionation of Iron and Iron(III)
iron-ferric-comproportionation-cell.description: When an iron nail is immersed in an iron(III) chloride solution, iron is oxidised while Fe³⁺ is reduced; the two oxidation states of the same element converge to give Fe²⁺ with heat release, and the solution colour changes from brown-yellow to pale green.
objectives: Understand the direction of electron transfer in a comproportionation reaction
Observe the colour change from brown-yellow to pale green
Learn to confirm the product by testing for Fe²⁺

tin-hydrochloric-hydrogen-electrode.title: Electrode Behaviour of Tin Reacting with Hydrochloric Acid to Produce Hydrogen Gas
tin-hydrochloric-hydrogen-electrode.description: A tin foil / tin sheet placed in hydrochloric acid evolves hydrogen gas slowly with a slight release of heat; the rate is markedly slower than that of magnesium or aluminium, reflecting that tin has an electrode potential closer to that of hydrogen.
objectives: Measure hydrogen gas evolution rates and rank them in order
Infer the relative electrode potentials from the observed rates
Master the technique of reading a gas-collection apparatus

nickel-hydrochloric-hydrogen-electrode.title: Electrode Behaviour of Nickel Reacting with Hydrochloric Acid to Produce Hydrogen Gas
nickel-hydrochloric-hydrogen-electrode.description: A nickel strip reacts with hydrochloric acid to release hydrogen gas slowly with a slight release of heat; comparing nickel with tin allows the electrode-potential order of several metals near hydrogen to be resolved more precisely.
objectives: Refine the electrode-potential sequence for metals close to hydrogen
Compare the hydrogen gas evolution rates of nickel and tin
Analyse how surface condition may interfere with the observed rate

zinc-nickel-chloride-displacement.title: Verification of the Activity Series: Zinc Displacing Nickel from Its Salt
zinc-nickel-chloride-displacement.description: Zinc granules added to a nickel(II) chloride solution displace grey nickel metal with heat release, and the green colour fades, confirming that zinc precedes nickel in the activity series.
objectives: Confirm the relative positions of zinc and nickel in the activity series
Observe the deposition of grey nickel metal
Learn to use the fading of colour as an indicator of decreasing ion concentration

iron-nickel-chloride-displacement.title: Verification of a Narrow Potential Gap: Iron Displacing Nickel from Its Salt
iron-nickel-chloride-displacement.description: An iron nail immersed in a nickel(II) chloride solution displaces nickel slowly with a slight release of heat; because the electrode-potential difference between the two metals is small, the reaction is sluggish and requires extended observation.
objectives: Observe the slow displacement reaction arising from a narrow potential gap
Record how the observable phenomena evolve over a prolonged period
Understand the distinction between thermodynamic feasibility and kinetic rate

magnesium-nickel-sulfate-displacement.title: Rapid Precipitation of Nickel by Magnesium in Nickel(II) Sulfate
magnesium-nickel-sulfate-displacement.description: When magnesium ribbon is placed in a nickel(II) sulfate solution, grey-black nickel precipitates rapidly and the temperature rises noticeably. Comparison with the iron–nickel pair highlights the effect of electrode potential difference on reaction rate.
objectives: Compare displacement rates at different electrode potential differences
Quantify the differences in temperature rise
Establish a qualitative relationship between reaction rate and electromotive force

zinc-cobalt-chloride-displacement.title: Verification of the Activity Series by Zinc Displacement of Cobalt(II) Chloride
zinc-cobalt-chloride-displacement.description: Zinc granules immersed in a cobalt(II) chloride solution displace grey cobalt with an accompanying release of heat; the pink colour of the solution gradually fades. This experiment may be placed alongside the nickel group to construct a segment of the activity series.
objectives: Confirm the relative activities of zinc and cobalt
Observe the fading of the pink colour and the deposition of cobalt
Complete the activity-series ranking of the three iron-group elements

cadmium-silver-nitrate-displacement.title: Dendritic Precipitation of Silver by Cadmium in Silver Nitrate
cadmium-silver-nitrate-displacement.description: When a cadmium sheet is placed in a silver nitrate solution, silvery-white dendrites grow on its surface and heat is released. The large electrode potential difference between cadmium and silver causes the deposition to proceed faster than in the lead–silver system.
objectives: Observe the dendritic morphology of silver deposited by cadmium displacement
Compare deposition rates at different electrode potential differences
Strictly follow cadmium handling and safety protocols

aluminum-silver-nitrate-displacement.title: Growth of a Silver Mirror by Aluminium Displacement in Silver Nitrate
aluminum-silver-nitrate-displacement.description: An aluminium strip from which the oxide film has been removed is immersed in a silver nitrate solution; a silvery-white coating forms on its surface rapidly and heat is released. This serves as a straightforward demonstration of electroless silver plating without an external power source.
objectives: Carry out chemical silver plating by the displacement method
Understand the effect of oxide-film removal on coating quality
Learn the correct procedure for recovering silver nitrate solution

nickel-copper-chloride-displacement.title: Anion Comparison: Nickel Displacement of Copper(II) Chloride
nickel-copper-chloride-displacement.description: A nickel strip immersed in a copper(II) chloride solution deposits red copper with a release of heat. The observation is consistent with results obtained using other copper salts, demonstrating that displacement depends solely on the electrode potential difference between the two metals and not on the nature of the anion.
objectives: Verify that the anion does not determine whether displacement occurs
Compare the reaction rates of two different copper salts
Summarise the determining factors of displacement reactions
